items.title: Pull Agoda hotel reviews with scores and sub-scores into a spreadsheet, in Python
items.summary: If you manage a hotel, run a reputation-management tool or analyse a city's hotel market, Agoda is one of the review sources you can't skip in Asia. A single hotel page there mixes two review pools: reviews from Agoda's own guests and reviews from Booking.com guests that Agoda republishes. Each pool has its own score, its own review count and its own six sub-scores (cleanliness, facilities, location, room comfort, service, value for money). Reading that by hand works for one property. For a competitive set of 20 hotels, checked every morning, it doesn't. This post pulls the reviews and scores into a CSV in Python and shows a daily "new reviews only" setup. Disclosure: I'm Aurelix, and I built Agoda API , an Agoda reviews scraper. It's a paid tool (prices below). What each row holds One row per review, from the hotel's public Agoda review page: source (Agoda or Booking.com), rating out of 10, rating_text , title , text , and for Booking.com-style reviews positives and negatives . language , plus original_title and original_text when Agoda shows an English translation, so you keep the guest's own words. review_date (the date the page shows), stay_month , nights , room_type , traveller_type (couple, solo, family, group, business). reviewer_name and reviewer_country as Agoda displays them, helpful_votes , photos . owner_response , owner_response_date and responder_name when the hotel replied. The hotel on every row: hotel_name , star_rating , address , city , country , agoda_score , agoda_review_count , agoda_sub_scores , agoda_score_distribution , booking_score , booking_review_count , booking_sub_scores . Hotels can be given as Agoda links (any language version), Agoda hotel IDs, or a hotel name with its city. A competitive set in one run pip install apify-client import csv import os from collections import defaultdict from apify_client import ApifyClient client = ApifyClient ( os . environ [ " APIFY_TOKEN " ]) run = client . actor ( " aurelix/agoda-reviews-scraper " ). call ( run_input = { " hotels " : [ " https://www.agoda.com/the-peninsula-bangkok/hotel/bangkok-th.html " , " Mandarin Oriental Bangkok " , " Shangri-La Bangkok " , ], " maxReviewsPerHotel " : 300 , " reviewsNewerThan " : " 90 days " , } ) reviews = list ( client . dataset ( run [ " defaultDatasetId " ]). iterate_items ()) fields = [ " hotel_name " , " source " , " rating " , " title " , " text " , " negatives " , " traveller_type " , " reviewer_country " , " review_date " , " owner_response " ] with open ( " reviews.csv " , " w " , newline = "" , encoding = " utf-8 " ) as f : w = csv . DictWriter ( f , fieldnames = fields , extrasaction = " ignore " ) w . writeheader () w . writerows ( reviews ) hotels = {} by_type = defaultdict ( list ) for r in reviews : hotels [ r [ " hotel_name " ]] = r by_type [( r [ " hotel_name " ], r [ " traveller_type " ])]. append ( r [ " rating " ]) for name , h in hotels . items (): subs = h [ " agoda_sub_scores " ] or {} print ( f " { name } : Agoda { h [ ' agoda_score ' ] } ( { h [ ' agoda_review_count ' ] } ratings), " f " Booking.com { h [ ' booking_score ' ] } ; cleanliness { subs . get ( ' Cleanliness ' ) } , " f " value { subs . get ( ' Value for money ' ) } " ) for ( name , kind ), ratings in sorted ( by_type . items ()): if kind and len ( ratings ) >= 5 : print ( f " { name } / { kind } : { sum ( ratings ) / len ( ratings ) : . 1 f } over { len ( ratings ) } reviews " ) The hotel name in the second line is matched through Agoda's own search box; the run's status message says which property each name matched, so check it once and switch to the link if it picked the wrong one. Ideas for the same data: Complaint mining : "maxRating": 6, "sortBy": "lowest" gives the unhappy reviews first; feed negatives and text to an LLM and ask for recurring themes per hotel. Reply rate : count rows with owner_response per hotel. It's a quick read on how actively each competitor manages its reviews. Who stays where : group by traveller_type and reviewer_country to see which segments each hotel attracts and how each segment rates it. New reviews every morning run_input = { " hotels " : [ " https://www.agoda.com/the-peninsula-bangkok/hotel/bangkok-th.html " , " ... " ], " maxReviewsPerHotel " : 500 , " onlyNewReviews " : True , " trackingName " : " my-compset-daily " , " slackWebhookUrl " : " https://hooks.slack.com/services/... " , } With onlyNewReviews on, the first run returns the newest reviews up to your limit, and later runs with the same trackingName return only reviews newer than the ones you already have: reading newest first, each review source stops at the first review you already received. A daily run over 20 hotels takes seconds and bills $0.0003 per hotel plus the new reviews. Save the input as a task in the Apify Console, schedule it daily, and the Slack URL gets the count and the top 10. Why this tool $0.50 per 1,000 reviews ($0.40 on paid plans), cheaper than the leading tools. Any number of hotels in one run, including by hotel name. The original text next to the translation. An only-new-reviews mode. What it doesn't cover: room prices and availability. Limits worth knowing Rows exist only for written reviews. The review counts next to the scores include rating-only reviews, so they are higher than the number of rows. Agoda's review service answers part of its requests with an empty page; the tool asks again before it decides a hotel has no more reviews, so long hotels take a little longer. "Highest" and "lowest rated first" follow Agoda's own order page by page; sort the CSV if you need a strict order across both review sources. The tool reads only what a logged-out visitor sees on Agoda's public review pages, never logs in, and returns reviewer names and countries exactly as Agoda shows them. Agoda's terms discourage automated access, so keep your use to analysing public reviews.
items.summary_html:
If you manage a hotel, run a reputation-management tool or analyse a city's hotel market, Agoda is one of the review sources you can't skip in Asia. A single hotel page there mixes two review pools: reviews from Agoda's own guests and reviews from Booking.com guests that Agoda republishes. Each pool has its own score, its own review count and its own six sub-scores (cleanliness, facilities, location, room comfort, service, value for money).

Reading that by hand works for one property. For a competitive set of 20 hotels, checked every morning, it doesn't. This post pulls the reviews and scores into a CSV in Python and shows a daily "new reviews only" setup.

Disclosure: I'm Aurelix, and I built Agoda API, an Agoda reviews scraper. It's a paid tool (prices below).

What each row holds

One row per review, from the hotel's public Agoda review page:

  • source (Agoda or Booking.com), rating out of 10, rating_text, title, text, and for Booking.com-style reviews positives and negatives.
  • language, plus original_title and original_text when Agoda shows an English translation, so you keep the guest's own words.
  • review_date (the date the page shows), stay_month, nights, room_type, traveller_type (couple, solo, family, group, business).
  • reviewer_name and reviewer_country as Agoda displays them, helpful_votes, photos.
  • owner_response, owner_response_date and responder_name when the hotel replied.
  • The hotel on every row: hotel_name, star_rating, address, city, country, agoda_score, agoda_review_count, agoda_sub_scores, agoda_score_distribution, booking_score, booking_review_count, booking_sub_scores.

Hotels can be given as Agoda links (any language version), Agoda hotel IDs, or a hotel name with its city.

A competitive set in one run 
pip install apify-client

import csv
import os
from collections import defaultdict

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])
run = client.actor("aurelix/agoda-reviews-scraper").call(
    run_input={
        "hotels": [
            "https://www.agoda.com/the-peninsula-bangkok/hotel/bangkok-th.html",
            "Mandarin Oriental Bangkok",
            "Shangri-La Bangkok",
        ],
        "maxReviewsPerHotel": 300,
        "reviewsNewerThan": "90 days",
    }
)
reviews = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())

fields = ["hotel_name", "source", "rating", "title", "text", "negatives", "traveller_type",
          "reviewer_country", "review_date", "owner_response"]
with open("reviews.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    w = csv.DictWriter(f, fieldnames=fields, extrasaction="ignore")
    w.writeheader()
    w.writerows(reviews)

hotels = {}
by_type = defaultdict(list)
for r in reviews:
    hotels[r["hotel_name"]] = r
    by_type[(r["hotel_name"], r["traveller_type"])].append(r["rating"])

for name, h in hotels.items():
    subs = h["agoda_sub_scores"] or {}
    print(f"{name}: Agoda {h['agoda_score']} ({h['agoda_review_count']} ratings), "
          f"Booking.com {h['booking_score']}; cleanliness {subs.get('Cleanliness')}, "
          f"value {subs.get('Value for money')}")
for (name, kind), ratings in sorted(by_type.items()):
    if kind and len(ratings) >= 5:
        print(f"  {name} / {kind}: {sum(ratings) / len(ratings):.1f} over {len(ratings)} reviews")

The hotel name in the second line is matched through Agoda's own search box; the run's status message says which property each name matched, so check it once and switch to the link if it picked the wrong one.

Ideas for the same data:

  • Complaint mining: "maxRating": 6, "sortBy": "lowest" gives the unhappy reviews first; feed negatives and text to an LLM and ask for recurring themes per hotel.
  • Reply rate: count rows with owner_response per hotel. It's a quick read on how actively each competitor manages its reviews.
  • Who stays where: group by traveller_type and reviewer_country to see which segments each hotel attracts and how each segment rates it.
New reviews every morning 
run_input = {
    "hotels": ["https://www.agoda.com/the-peninsula-bangkok/hotel/bangkok-th.html", "..."],
    "maxReviewsPerHotel": 500,
    "onlyNewReviews": True,
    "trackingName": "my-compset-daily",
    "slackWebhookUrl": "https://hooks.slack.com/services/...",
}

With onlyNewReviews on, the first run returns the newest reviews up to your limit, and later runs with the same trackingName return only reviews newer than the ones you already have: reading newest first, each review source stops at the first review you already received. A daily run over 20 hotels takes seconds and bills $0.0003 per hotel plus the new reviews. Save the input as a task in the Apify Console, schedule it daily, and the Slack URL gets the count and the top 10.

Why this tool
  • $0.50 per 1,000 reviews ($0.40 on paid plans), cheaper than the leading tools.
  • Any number of hotels in one run, including by hotel name.
  • The original text next to the translation.
  • An only-new-reviews mode.
  • What it doesn't cover: room prices and availability.
Limits worth knowing
  • Rows exist only for written reviews. The review counts next to the scores include rating-only reviews, so they are higher than the number of rows.
  • Agoda's review service answers part of its requests with an empty page; the tool asks again before it decides a hotel has no more reviews, so long hotels take a little longer.
  • "Highest" and "lowest rated first" follow Agoda's own order page by page; sort the CSV if you need a strict order across both review sources.

The tool reads only what a logged-out visitor sees on Agoda's public review pages, never logs in, and returns reviewer names and countries exactly as Agoda shows them. Agoda's terms discourage automated access, so keep your use to analysing public reviews.

items.title: The Physical Nightmare of On-Device AI: Why Your LLM Fails on a Custom PCB
items.summary: In 2026, the hottest buzzword in the tech world is undoubtedly "On-Device AI." From Apple Intelligence to the flood of AI PCs and AI smartphones hitting the market, the entire software industry is racing to cram large language models (LLMs) and vision models—previously running in the cloud—into portable devices weighing just a few dozen grams. As a software engineer, you might have fine-tuned models on a workstation with a dedicated GPU or run flawless inference in the cloud. But when your team moves to mass production and deploys the model onto a custom PCBA (Printed Circuit Board Assembly) you designed yourselves, the nightmare begins. The device gets burning hot, the battery drains in minutes, inference speed turns from silky smooth into a slideshow, and the system crashes and reboots repeatedly. I work at AnyPCBA, a manufacturer specializing in small-to-medium volume PCB and PCBA production. I frequently see software AI teams hit the wall of physical reality. Today, from the manufacturing perspective, let's dive deep into the three biggest "physical disasters" developers overlook when deploying on-device AI. 1. Peak Compute ≠ Sustained Compute (The Brutal Reality of Thermal Throttling) Software developers look at chip specs and fixate on TOPS (Trillions of Operations Per Second). For example, an edge NPU claims 20 TOPS, and you assume it's more than enough to run your lightweight model. But in the physical world, a chip cannot sustain its 20 TOPS peak indefinitely. When the NPU runs full-load LLM inference, it generates an astonishing heat flux density (reaching dozens of watts per square centimeter) on a few square millimeters of silicon. If your PCB design lacks large thermal copper pours, dense thermal via arrays, or external heatsinks, the chip temperature will skyrocket past 100°C within minutes. At this point, the chip's self-protection mechanism forces Thermal Throttling . Your model might run smoothly for the first 10 seconds, then drop to a slideshow, or simply reboot due to overheat protection. AnyPCBA's Solution: During DFM review, we recommend AI hardware teams use high-Tg materials and design large exposed thermal pads with dense via arrays directly beneath the NPU. Copper conducts heat 1,300 times faster than FR-4 substrate. Only through precise via plating processes can heat be rapidly conducted to the backside heatsink or liquid cooling module. Without proper physical thermal management, even the most powerful compute is meaningless. 2. Instantaneous Current Draw Leads to a "False OOM" (Voltage Droop) In the cloud, if you run out of memory, you hit an OOM (Out of Memory). On edge hardware, you'll encounter a similar crash— Voltage Droop . When an AI chip executes dense tensor operations, it draws tens of amps in microseconds from a low-power sleep state (extremely high di/dt). If your PCB's Power Delivery Network (PDN) can't respond fast enough—because decoupling capacitors are too far from the chip pins or trace parasitic inductance (ESL) is too high—the local supply voltage will collapse instantly. The result: logic gates fail, and the chip crashes and reboots. This "false OOM" cannot be fixed by changing code. AnyPCBA's Solution: PDN design for AI hardware is extremely demanding. We not only place 0201 or even 01005 decoupling capacitors as close as possible to the chip pins, but also use thinner dielectric layers to increase plane capacitance, pushing PDN impedance to extremely low levels—ensuring instant high current is delivered on demand. 3. The "Invisible Ceiling" of Memory Bandwidth and SI Disasters On a PC or server, you rarely worry about memory bandwidth. But on edge devices, it's a fatal bottleneck. LLM inference is a classic "memory-bound" task. No matter how powerful the compute, if memory can't feed it, everything is moot. Worse, data exchange between LPDDR memory and the main chip relies heavily on PCB traces. If length matching and impedance control are not precisely executed, data will experience phase skew and bit errors. From the software layer, the model suddenly outputs garbage or crashes. AnyPCBA's Solution: High-speed memory traces (such as LPDDR5/DDR5) must strictly meet 100Ω or 90Ω differential impedance requirements with precise length matching. Our engineering team uses TDR (Time Domain Reflectometry) testing before production to ensure signal integrity on the physical copper traces—so hardware weaknesses never drag down your algorithm. 4. The Limits of Physical Space: The Power Conflict That Can't "Pop Up" In software, if two threads compete for resources, the OS can schedule them. In hardware, the routing space for power and ground is physically fixed. The mainboards in AI phones or smart glasses are extremely compact. High-speed signals, high-current power lines, and sensitive analog sensors are forced into a few square centimeters. If layout is poor, the switching noise from high current will directly couple onto analog signal lines, causing sensor data to be completely corrupted. AnyPCBA's Solution: During layout, we strictly partition "Analog Ground (AGND)" and "Digital Ground (DGND)," adding proper shielding and isolation between power and ground planes. On the manufacturing side, we use blind/buried vias (HDI) with laser-drilled microvias to achieve more interconnections in limited space, avoiding signal interference. Conclusion: Bridging the Boundary Between Algorithm and Physics Deploying on-device AI is never purely a software problem. It's an ultimate battle between algorithms and thermodynamics, electronics, and materials science. At AnyPCBA, we frequently help edge AI teams with DFM (Design for Manufacturing) reviews. We don't just understand PCB manufacturing—we understand how to turn your algorithm into hardware that runs stably in a user's pocket. If you're developing AI PCs, smart wearables, or edge computing devices, and your model works great on a dev board but crashes on your custom PCB, contact us through our website. What's the most absurd thermal or crash issue you've encountered in edge AI hardware development? Share your experience in the comments.

items.title: Tokenization: BPE from Scratch, Vocab Size, and What Tokenizers Hide
items.summary: Tokenization: BPE from Scratch, Vocab Size, and What Tokenizers Hide Before a language model reads a single word, a tokenizer has already decided how that word gets cut up. The model never sees letters. It never sees words either. It sees token IDs, numbers drawn from a fixed list, and everything the model can and cannot do starts with that list. We built byte pair encoding from scratch, trained it on 83,159 real words from our own published articles, and measured it against OpenAI's real tokenizers. The headline numbers: the same sentence costs 16 tokens in English and 60 in Urdu, a vocabulary stops paying for itself after about 5,000 merges, and the number 2026 is two tokens because the tokenizer chops digits into groups of three. This is Deep Part 2 of the AI Engineer Deep series, and it goes one layer deeper than Part 3 of the original series, How LLMs Actually Work , where we first showed that tokens, not words, are what you pay for. The 30-second answer Tokenization turns text into a sequence of integer IDs using a fixed vocabulary built by byte pair encoding, or BPE. BPE starts from single characters and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token until the vocabulary reaches its target size. Frequent words stay whole, rare words split into pieces, and any word at all can be represented because the vocabulary always contains single characters as a fallback. The size of that vocabulary is a real engineering tradeoff: a bigger vocabulary packs text into fewer tokens, which saves money and context, but every extra token adds a row to the embedding matrix, which costs parameters. And because the vocabulary is learned from data, it carries the biases of that data: English is cheap, Urdu is expensive, and a handful of tokens in every vocabulary were barely trained at all. Where BPE came from BPE started life as a compression algorithm. Philip Gage described it in 1994 as a way to squeeze data by repeatedly replacing the most frequent pair of bytes with a single unused byte. It sat in compression textbooks for twenty years until Rico Sennrich, Barry Haddow, and Alexandra Birch adapted it for neural machine translation in their 2016 paper, Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units. Their problem was concrete: word-level translation models had fixed vocabularies, so rare words became an unknown token and the model had nothing to say about them. BPE fixed that by letting any word be spelled out as a sequence of frequent pieces. On the WMT 2015 English to German and English to Russian tasks, their subword models beat a word-level model with a back-off dictionary by up to 1.1 and 1.3 BLEU. That is a modest number on paper and a large idea in practice: the same greedy merge loop now sits at the front of every major language model, from GPT-2 to Llama 3. The experiment: BPE from scratch on the paper's own toy corpus We implemented the exact algorithm from the Sennrich paper in plain Python, no libraries, and ran it on the paper's own example dictionary: low (5 times), lowest (2), newer (6), wider (3), new (2). The algorithm counts every adjacent symbol pair weighted by word frequency, merges the most frequent pair everywhere, and repeats. Ten merges in, the vocabulary already looks like a real tokenizer in miniature. MergePair mergedResultCount 1e + rer9 2er + end of worder9 3n + ene8 4ne + wnew8 5l + olo7 6lo + wlow7 7new + ernewer6 8low + end of wordlow5 9w + iwi3 10wi + dwid3 After ten merges, the frequent words are whole tokens and the rare ones are pieces: low is one token, newer is one token, lowest splits into low plus e plus s plus t, and wider splits into wid plus er. That is the whole trick. Nothing in the algorithm knows English. It only knows frequency. The code is short enough to read in one sitting, and it is the same loop that builds production vocabularies, just with a smaller corpus and fewer merges. import collections def get_pair_stats ( vocab , freq ): pairs = collections . defaultdict ( int ) for word , symbols in vocab . items (): for i in range ( len ( symbols ) - 1 ): pairs [( symbols [ i ], symbols [ i + 1 ])] += freq [ word ] return pairs def merge_pair ( pair , vocab ): out = {} bigram = "" . join ( pair ) for word , symbols in vocab . items (): i , merged = 0 , [] while i " ] for w in corpus} for step in range(10): pairs = get_pair_stats(vocab, corpus) best = max(pairs, key=pairs.get) vocab = merge_pair(best, vocab) The experiment: training BPE on 83,159 real words A toy corpus proves the loop works. It says nothing about scale, so we trained the same code on every word in our own published articles: 83,159 words, 6,233 unique. Then we encoded a held out sentence the tokenizer had never seen, 25 words about tokenizers themselves, and measured how many tokens it took as the vocabulary grew. MergesVocabulary sizeTokens for the held out sentenceCharacters per token 0271390.99 100127692.00 500527433.21 2,0002,027304.60 5,0005,027255.52 10,0009,958255.52 Two things stand out. First, the early merges do almost all the work: the first 100 merges cut the token count in half, and 2,000 merges get you to 4.60 characters per token. Second, the curve flattens hard. Going from 5,000 merges to 10,000 merges bought exactly zero fewer tokens on held out text, because the extra merges memorized quirks of our training articles instead of learning general pieces. A bigger vocabulary is not automatically a better tokenizer. It is a bigger vocabulary that has to earn its keep on text it has never seen. At 2,000 merges, our little tokenizer split unseen words the way a real one would: tokenizer became tokeniz plus er, unbelievable became un plus be plus li plus ev plus able, and transformers became trans plus form plus ers. The 45 letter word pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis fell apart into 21 small pieces, which is exactly what should happen to a word the tokenizer has never met. The experiment: OpenAI's real tokenizers on real text Our toy BPE proves the mechanism. To see what production tokenizers actually do, we ran the same text through tiktoken, OpenAI's own BPE library, with three real encodings: r50k_base from GPT-2, cl100k_base from GPT-4, and o200k_base from GPT-4o. A 196 character paragraph about attention took 39 tokens under all three, or 5.03 characters per token. On plain English prose, three generations of tokenizer agree almost exactly. The differences show up the moment you leave English. LanguageSame sentence, charactersTokens (cl100k_base)Characters per token English73164.56 German86263.31 Chinese19280.68 Urdu63601.05 The same meaning costs 16 tokens in English and 60 in Urdu, a 3.75x multiplier, and Chinese needs 28 tokens for a 19 character sentence because each character carries a whole syllable of meaning and still splits into more than one token. This is not a rounding error. It is a price difference. Every API call is billed per token, every context window is measured in tokens, and a user writing in Urdu pays nearly four times as much as a user writing the same thing in English, for the same model and the same answer. Published analyses of token pricing across languages have found gaps as large as 10x for some languages. Our own measurement sits inside that range, and it is the reason newer vocabularies keep growing: o200k_base roughly doubles cl100k_base to about 200,019 tokens, and Llama 3 moved to 128,256 tokens, largely to buy back efficiency in non English text. Numbers: the tokenizer chops digits into groups of three Numbers get special treatment, and it explains a famous model weakness. Under cl100k_base, 123456789 becomes three tokens, 123 plus 456 plus 789. The year 2026 becomes two tokens, 202 plus 6. Pi to fourteen decimal places becomes seven tokens, 3 plus a dot plus 141 plus 592 plus 653 plus 589 plus 79. The model never sees a number as a number. It sees digit chunks of up to three, glued together by position. That is why a model can write a poem about arithmetic and still fumble a five digit addition: the digits it must add were never presented as a single unit. The same blindness shows up in spelling. Ask a model how many r letters are in strawberry, and remember that it never sees the word strawberry. It sees str plus aw plus berry, three tokens, and the letter r is smeared across token boundaries the model cannot inspect. The failure is not in the model's reasoning. It is in the input representation, and no amount of prompting fixes a representation problem. Vocab size: the tradeoff nobody prices Every token in the vocabulary costs parameters twice over: once in the input embedding matrix that turns IDs into vectors, and once in the output head that turns vectors back into probabilities over the vocabulary. For GPT-2 small, the embedding matrix is 50,257 tokens times 768 dimensions, about 38.6 million parameters, or 31.1 percent of the whole 124 million parameter model. For Llama 3 8B, the matrix is 128,256 tokens times 4,096 dimensions, about 525 million parameters, or 6.6 percent of the model. The share falls as models grow, but the absolute cost never goes away, and a vocabulary of 262,145 tokens like Gemma 3 pays for it in both matrices. This is the real reason vocabularies do not grow without limit. A bigger vocabulary compresses text better, which saves context and money on every request, but it also makes the model bigger, slower to load, and more expensive to train, and our sweep shows the compression gain flattens long before the parameter cost does. Picking a vocabulary size is picking a point on that curve, and most teams pick it once and live with it for the life of the model. What tokenizers hide Three things about tokenizers surprise working engineers, and all three follow from how BPE is actually built. First, tokenization happens before the model, and it happens in two steps: a regex first splits text into chunks, then BPE merges inside each chunk. The regex decides that a leading space belongs to the following word, which is why hello world is two tokens, hello and space plus world, and why tokenization with a leading space is two tokens, space plus token and ization. Change the space and you change the tokens, which is why the same word can tokenize differently at the start of a sentence and in the middle of one. Second, the tokenizer and the model are trained separately, on different data, and that gap creates glitch tokens. A string that was frequent in the tokenizer's training text earns its own token, but if it barely appears in the model's training text, its embedding never gets trained. The famous case is SolidGoldMagikarp, a Reddit username that appeared in so many counting threads that GPT-2's tokenizer gave it a token of its own, while the model itself almost never saw it in training. Asked to repeat it, GPT-2 era models produced evasions, insults, or unrelated text. We verified the fix with tiktoken: the old r50k_base encoding splits it into two tokens, Solid and GoldMagikarp, and both cl100k_base and o200k_base split it into five, Solid plus Gold plus Mag plus ik plus arp. A 2024 paper by Land and Bartolo, Fishing for Magikarp, showed these undertrained tokens are common across many open model families and can be found automatically. Third, tokenizers are frozen the day the model ships. You cannot add a token for your product name, your file format, or your language without retraining the model, so every prompt you write is at the mercy of merge decisions made months or years ago on someone else's corpus. Our opinionated take Most teams treat the tokenizer as plumbing and never look at it, and that is a mistake we think costs real money. If you build on top of language models, the tokenizer is the first thing you should measure, not the last. Count tokens before you count dollars: our paragraph of English cost 39 tokens, and one million tokens of English prose is roughly five megabytes of text, so a retrieval pipeline that stuffs whole documents into context is paying a token bill it never budgeted for. Test your prompts in the languages your users actually write, because a 3.75x token multiplier is a 3.75x cost multiplier and a 3.75x smaller effective context window, and no one will tell you that until the invoice arrives. And if you train anything yourself, do not chase the biggest vocabulary you can afford. Our sweep flattened at 5,000 merges on real text, and the production lesson is the same: the vocabulary that wins is the one trained on your data, sized to the point where the curve bends, not the biggest number on a spec sheet. The tokenizer is the cheapest part of the model to understand and the most expensive part to ignore. Tokenization: BPE from Scratch, Vocab Size, and What Tokenizers Hide

Before a language model reads a single word, a tokenizer has already decided how that word gets cut up. The model never sees letters. It never sees words either. It sees token IDs, numbers drawn from a fixed list, and everything the model can and cannot do starts with that list. We built byte pair encoding from scratch, trained it on 83,159 real words from our own published articles, and measured it against OpenAI's real tokenizers. This is Deep Part 2 of the AI Engineer Deep series, and it goes one layer deeper than Part 3 of the original series, How LLMs Actually Work, where we first showed that tokens, not words, are what you pay for.

The 30-second answer

Tokenization turns text into a sequence of integer IDs using a fixed vocabulary built by byte pair encoding, or BPE. BPE starts from single characters and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token until the vocabulary reaches its target size. Frequent words stay whole, rare words split into pieces, and any word at all can be represented because the vocabulary always contains single characters as a fallback. The size of that vocabulary is a real engineering tradeoff: a bigger vocabulary packs text into fewer tokens, which saves money and context, but every extra token adds a row to the embedding matrix, which costs parameters. And because the vocabulary is learned from data, it carries the biases of that data: English is cheap, Urdu is expensive, and a handful of tokens in every vocabulary were barely trained at all.

Where BPE came from

BPE started life as a compression algorithm. Philip Gage described it in 1994 as a way to squeeze data by repeatedly replacing the most frequent pair of bytes with a single unused byte. It sat in compression textbooks for twenty years until Rico Sennrich, Barry Haddow, and Alexandra Birch adapted it for neural machine translation in their 2016 paper, Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units. Their problem was concrete: word-level translation models had fixed vocabularies, so rare words became an unknown token and the model had nothing to say about them. BPE fixed that by letting any word be spelled out as a sequence of frequent pieces. On the WMT 2015 English to German and English to Russian tasks, their subword models beat a word-level model with a back-off dictionary by up to 1.1 and 1.3 BLEU. That is a modest number on paper and a large idea in practice: the same greedy merge loop now sits at the front of every major language model, from GPT-2 to Llama 3.

We implemented the exact algorithm from the Sennrich paper in plain Python, no libraries, and ran it on the paper's own example dictionary: low (5 times), lowest (2), newer (6), wider (3), new (2). items.title: Darwin-180B-RSI-R3: Open-Weight MoE Scores #2 on SuperCLUE Math & Science Reasoning, Beating Gemini and Grok
items.summary: Darwin-180B-RSI-R3: Open-Weight MoE Scores #2 on SuperCLUE Math & Science Reasoning, Beating Gemini and Grok TL;DR: Darwin-180B-RSI-R3 is a 180-billion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model from VIDRAFT that scored 73.68 on the SuperCLUE November 2026 math and science reasoning dimension — ranking #2 overall and #1 among open-weight models on an independently administered, non-public test. It activates only ~3B parameters per token, ships weights under a Qwen community license permitting commercial use, and has a 4-bit quantized variant that runs on a 32 GB RAM laptop without a GPU. What it is Darwin-180B-RSI-R3 is a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language model built on top of Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next as a base. Key facts from the source: Parameter count: 180B total, with roughly 3B activated per token at inference time Architecture lineage: Inherits the expert layers from Qwen3.8-Flash-Next — 512 experts per layer, with the bulk of world knowledge stored in those feed-forward network (FFN) blocks What changed vs. the base: Only the attention layers, linear-attention layers, and shared expert layers were retrained using a self-improvement process; the FFN expert blocks were kept intact License: Qwen community license, open-weight, commercial use permitted Edge variant: POCKET-Darwin-180B-GGUF — a 4-bit quantized GGUF version designed to run from SSD on a 32 GB RAM consumer laptop, no GPU required Developer: VIDRAFT (South Korean Pre-AGI AI startup) The model was independently evaluated by SuperCLUE on November 5, 2026. SuperCLUE is a Chinese LLM benchmark that evolved from the 2019 CLUE (Chinese Language Understanding Evaluation) project. It issues fresh, non-public test sets each month and scores models across five dimensions: agentic coding, math & science reasoning, hallucination suppression, precise instruction following, and long-context understanding. How it works The core idea behind Darwin-180B-RSI-R3 is surgical retraining : instead of fine-tuning an entire large model, VIDRAFT preserved the FFN expert layers — which encode the model's factual and domain knowledge — and exclusively retrained the components most responsible for multi-step reasoning: the attention layers, linear-attention layers, and shared experts. The retraining mechanism is described in Korean media coverage as a self-improvement loop : the model generates its own problems, produces candidate answers, verifies those answers internally, and uses that feedback signal to update weights. This is conceptually similar to self-play or self-distillation approaches common in the reasoning research literature, applied specifically to the layers governing how the model attends to and routes information rather than what it knows . The practical consequence of this design choice: the same 512-expert FFN knowledge base as the parent model, but with reasoning-focused layers optimized through iterative self-generated supervision. Benchmarks & results All numbers below come directly from the SuperCLUE November 2026 leaderboard (published 2026-11-05) and are independently administered — not self-reported by VIDRAFT. Metric Score / Rank SuperCLUE Math & Science Reasoning 73.68 (2nd of 19 models) SuperCLUE Math & Science Reasoning — open-weight rank #1 SuperCLUE 5-dimension composite index 43.08 (9th of 19 models, 5th among open-weight) GPQA Diamond (Hugging Face leaderboard) 94.44 (ranked #1 at time of reporting) Score delta vs. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next base (math & science reasoning) +15.8 points Composite rank improvement vs. base +6 positions The model ranked above Google Gemini, xAI's Grok, and DeepSeek on the math & science reasoning dimension. The only model ahead of it was GPT-6.1-Sol at 76.32. Important context: SuperCLUE places non-Chinese models on the same table for reference but does not include them in its official ranking. The 73.68 score is from a held-out, non-public November test set — not a contamination-prone static benchmark. How to try it The source article confirms that model weights are publicly available. Based on the information reported: Weights: Released under the Qwen community license (commercial use allowed). Check the VIDRAFT organization page on Hugging Face for Darwin-180B-RSI-R3 . Edge/CPU variant: POCKET-Darwin-180B-GGUF (4-bit quantized) is designed for 32 GB RAM laptops running inference from SSD — no GPU required. Look for it on Hugging Face under VIDRAFT's model hub. The source does not publicly document a specific API endpoint, GitHub repository URL, or installation command for this release. Check VIDRAFT's official channels for the latest access instructions before deployment. FAQ Q: Why does the model score #2 on reasoning but only #9 overall on SuperCLUE? A: Darwin-180B-RSI-R3 was specifically optimized for math and science reasoning. The five-dimension SuperCLUE composite also includes agentic coding, hallucination suppression, instruction following, and long-context tasks — areas where the model was not specifically retrained. The result is a narrow specialist that excels on its target dimension while sitting mid-table overall. Q: Is retraining only the attention layers a proven approach, or experimental? A: The approach is conceptually grounded in existing research showing that FFN layers store factual knowledge while attention layers govern reasoning and information routing. The +15.8-point gain on an independently scored, non-public benchmark is a concrete external data point, though a single benchmark result should always be interpreted alongside broader evaluation. Q: Can I run the full 180B model on consumer hardware? A: Not the full-precision model. The POCKET-Darwin-180B-GGUF 4-bit quantized variant is specifically designed for 32 GB RAM laptops running from SSD without a GPU, according to the source coverage. Q: Does the Qwen community license allow me to use this in a commercial product? A: The source states commercial use is permitted under the Qwen community license. Always review the full license text in the model repository before production deployment. Originally reported by 넷이즈 网易 (중국) (2026-11-07) — source article .

Darwin-180B-RSI-R3: Open-Weight MoE Scores #2 on SuperCLUE Math & Science Reasoning, Beating Gemini and Grok

TL;DR: Darwin-180B-RSI-R3 is a 180-billion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model from VIDRAFT that scored 73.68 on the SuperCLUE November 2026 math and science reasoning dimension — ranking #2 overall and #1 among open-weight models on an independently administered, non-public test. It activates only ~3B parameters per token, ships weights under a Qwen community license permitting commercial use, and has a 4-bit quantized variant that runs on a 32 GB RAM laptop without a GPU.

What it is

Darwin-180B-RSI-R3 is a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language model built on top of Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next as a base. Key facts from the source:

  • Parameter count: 180B total, with roughly 3B activated per token at inference time
  • Architecture lineage: Inherits the expert layers from Qwen3.8-Flash-Next — 512 experts per layer, with the bulk of world knowledge stored in those feed-forward network (FFN) blocks
  • What changed vs. the base: Only the attention layers, linear-attention layers, and shared expert layers were retrained using a self-improvement process; the FFN expert blocks were kept intact
  • License: Qwen community license, open-weight, commercial use permitted
  • Edge variant: POCKET-Darwin-180B-GGUF — a 4-bit quantized GGUF version designed to run from SSD on a 32 GB RAM consumer laptop, no GPU required
  • Developer: VIDRAFT (South Korean Pre-AGI AI startup)

The model was independently evaluated by SuperCLUE on November 5, 2026. SuperCLUE is a Chinese LLM benchmark that evolved from the 2019 CLUE (Chinese Language Understanding Evaluation) project. It issues fresh, non-public test sets each month and scores models across five dimensions: agentic coding, math & science reasoning, hallucination suppression, precise instruction following, and long-context understanding.

How it works

The core idea behind Darwin-180B-RSI-R3 is surgical retraining: instead of fine-tuning an entire large model, VIDRAFT preserved the FFN expert layers — which encode the model's factual and domain knowledge — and exclusively retrained the components most responsible for multi-step reasoning: the attention layers, linear-attention layers, and shared experts.

The retraining mechanism is described in Korean media coverage as a self-improvement loop: the model generates its own problems, produces candidate answers, verifies those answers internally, and uses that feedback signal to update weights. This is conceptually similar to self-play or self-distillation approaches common in the reasoning research literature, applied specifically to the layers governing how the model attends to and routes information rather than what it knows.

The practical consequence of this design choice: the same 512-expert FFN knowledge base as the parent model, but with reasoning-focused layers optimized through iterative self-generated supervision.

Benchmarks & results

All numbers below come directly from the SuperCLUE November 2026 leaderboard (published 2026-11-05) and are independently administered — not self-reported by VIDRAFT.

Metric Score / Rank SuperCLUE Math & Science Reasoning 73.68 (2nd of 19 models) SuperCLUE Math & Science Reasoning — open-weight rank #1 SuperCLUE 5-dimension composite index 43.08 (9th of 19 models, 5th among open-weight) GPQA Diamond (Hugging Face leaderboard) 94.44 (ranked #1 at time of reporting) Score delta vs. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next base (math & science reasoning) +15.8 points Composite rank improvement vs. base +6 positions

The model ranked above Google Gemini, xAI's Grok, and DeepSeek on the math & science reasoning dimension. The only model ahead of it was GPT-6.1-Sol at 76.32.

Important context: SuperCLUE places non-Chinese models on the same table for reference but does not include them in its official ranking. The 73.68 score is from a held-out, non-public November test set — not a contamination-prone static benchmark.

How to try it

The source article confirms that model weights are publicly available. Based on the information reported:

  • Weights: Released under the Qwen community license (commercial use allowed). Check the VIDRAFT organization page on Hugging Face for Darwin-180B-RSI-R3.
  • Edge/CPU variant: POCKET-Darwin-180B-GGUF (4-bit quantized) is designed for 32 GB RAM laptops running inference from SSD — no GPU required. Look for it on Hugging Face under VIDRAFT's model hub.

The source does not publicly document a specific API endpoint, GitHub repository URL, or installation command for this release. Check VIDRAFT's official channels for the latest access instructions before deployment.

FAQ

Q: Why does the model score #2 on reasoning but only #9 overall on SuperCLUE?
A: Darwin-180B-RSI-R3 was specifically optimized for math and science reasoning. The five-dimension SuperCLUE composite also includes agentic coding, hallucination suppression, instruction following, and long-context tasks — areas where the model was not specifically retrained. The result is a narrow specialist that excels on its target dimension while sitting mid-table overall.

Q: Is retraining only the attention layers a proven approach, or experimental?
A: The approach is conceptually grounded in existing research showing that FFN layers store factual knowledge while attention layers govern reasoning and information routing. The +15.8-point gain on an independently scored, non-public benchmark is a concrete external data point, though a single benchmark result should always be interpreted alongside broader evaluation.

Q: Can I run the full 180B model on consumer hardware?
A: Not the full-precision model. The POCKET-Darwin-180B-GGUF 4-bit quantized variant is specifically designed for 32 GB RAM laptops running from SSD without a GPU, according to the source coverage.

Q: Does the Qwen community license allow me to use this in a commercial product?
A: The source states commercial use is permitted under the Qwen community license. Always review the full license text in the model repository before production deployment.

items.title: How to plan an infrastructure task without losing your mind: a breakdown using an AWS deployment as an example
items.summary: The ticket fits on one line: "deploy a new web service to AWS and add jobs to deploy it." Inside that line are a network, containers, a database, secrets, a CDN, two workflows and dozens of small steps that an engineer usually keeps in their head. That works while nothing interrupts you. Then you join a call, come back, and can't remember whether you checked the security group. And when someone asks how long it will take, the honest answer is "a day or two." I've been building IT infrastructure for about 15 years, and today I lead a DevOps team at a game studio. Tasks like "spin up a new service" or "change system X" land on my desk every week, and over the years I've settled into a fairly stable way of planning them. I tried to write that method down and then give it to an agent. Part 1. How an engineer plans a task The task Let's take a concrete one: Deploy a new web service to AWS. It has a React frontend and a Python backend, and requires PostgreSQL to run. The application repository is github.com/javdet/nib-demo-app . This should result in jobs in GitHub for deploying the infrastructure and the application. Nothing unusual. Tasks like this come in all the time, and anyone who works with infrastructure has a rough idea of what's behind them. Let's walk through what happens in an engineer's head when this ticket arrives, step by step and slower than it happens in real life. Step 1. Collect context Before planning anything, the engineer answers three questions: What is the project? Who uses it, how critical it is, whether it has environments besides production. How does the current infrastructure work? Which AWS accounts exist, where the Terraform state lives, how the networks are laid out, what CI/CD is already there. What do we know about the products in the task? Here that's AWS, PostgreSQL and GitHub Actions: which AWS services fit, which Postgres version to use, how Actions will reach the cloud. Some of the answers are already in their head. The rest they pull from git and the wiki: usually details of how the infrastructure is built and the company's internal rules for cloud, databases and CI/CD. This step already shows the first problem, and we'll come back to it: a large part of the context isn't written down anywhere except in one person's head. Step 2. Outline the stages Once the context is collected, the task falls apart into large stages: Write infrastructure code for the AWS resources. Write the build and deploy workflows. Create the resources in AWS. Deploy the application. Check that everything works. The stages depend on each other: you can't deploy the app before the cluster exists, and you can't create the cluster before the code exists. The dependencies matter more than the list itself, because they decide what can run in parallel and what can't. Step 3. Break the stages into basic actions Each stage is a set of simple actions you can do in one go: edit a file; run a CLI command; make an API call; change a setting in a UI. For example, "create the resources in AWS" becomes a chain: create a bucket for the state, give GitHub Actions access to the account, run terraform plan , read the diff, run terraform apply , look at the outputs. Step 4. Lean on rules and experience To put the actions in the right order, the engineer relies on two things: Team rules. How we name resources, where we keep state, which tags are required, what we never do in production. Their own experience. They've done something similar before and remember where it hurt last time. ### Step 5. Build the plan: action, check, rollback These pieces add up to a detailed plan. Usually it lives in the engineer's head, less often on paper. A good plan has three parts: actions : what exactly we do; checks before closing each stage: how to know the stage is really done, and not just "seems fine"; a rollback plan in case something goes wrong. The Rollback column is the one people leave empty most often. Be honest: when did you last write a rollback plan before you needed it? Step 6. Execute Then the engineer walks the whole list: action, check, action, check. If a check fails, they roll back or fix the problem, and check again. Tedious, right? Where this process breaks On paper it's a good process. In practice it breaks in three places. 1. The action list lives in your head, and items fall out of it. A call, an alert, a colleague asking you to look at their PR. An hour later you come back to the task and you're no longer sure whether you closed the database port to the internet. A plan in your head doesn't survive context switches, and you can't hand it to a colleague if you get sick in the middle of the task. This happened to me when I was moving asset buckets from one cloud to another. I copied the data and set up access, but forgot to add CORS. It's a couple of lines of config, and it feels so obvious that it never makes it onto any list. 2. Checks get skipped. You want to save time: "the site opened, so it works." The fact that the database is reachable from the internet, or that backups aren't set up, comes up a month later. Checks are the first thing to go under a deadline, because skipping them doesn't break anything right away. 3. Nobody knows how big the task is. Ask "how long will it take?" and you hear "a day or two." That's not an estimate. Until the task is broken into actions, its size is invisible: to you, to your team lead, and to whoever filed the ticket. All three have the same cause: the plan exists only in the head of the person doing the work, so you can't hand it over and you can't measure it. What if an agent builds the plan? So here's the natural question: what if an agent does the breakdown, the planning, the execution and the checks? The engineer still controls the stages, decides which steps to run, and accepts the final result. That's why I built nib (Neuro Infrastructure Builder). It's a tool for infrastructure work: it splits a task into stages, writes concrete actions with checks for each stage, builds a rollback plan, and then either runs the steps itself or gives the operator detailed instructions. Inside, nib follows the same logic as the engineer from Part 1. The work is split into modes, and each mode has its own role: The context, rules and experience the engineer relies on exist in nib too: a knowledge base, rules and skills. In this post we only use the knowledge base. The rest is a topic for the next part. Part 2. From git clone to a working site Now let's run the same task through nib. The whole run is on video : What you need Docker; an API key for an LLM provider. nib works with any OpenAI-compatible API, and the installer has presets for OpenAI, OpenRouter, Google Gemini, Qwen, DeepSeek, Grok and Kimi; an AWS account. I strongly recommend a separate sandbox account: the agent will need keys that can create resources; a GitHub account and a fork of demo-app , if you want to repeat this exact task. Installation nib runs locally with Docker Compose or in Kubernetes with a Helm chart. The local option is enough to try it: git clone https://github.com/javdet/nib.git cd nib make setup make setup is an interactive script. It asks for the LLM provider, the model and the key (I use OpenRouter), then the name of your first project and, optionally, its environments, clouds and regions. You can skip those fields, but nib plans better with them, and you can add more projects later. Then the script generates tokens, writes .env and the config, and starts four containers: Postgres, the knowledge base server, the backend and the frontend. At the end it prints the UI address ( http://localhost:8080 by default; if the port is busy, it picks a free one) and an API token. You paste this token on the login screen. It's also saved in .env as NIB_API_TOKEN , so it's hard to lose. Knowledge base: what to fill in for a new project The first place to open after you log in is Knowledgebase . This is the "context" from step 1: everything the engineer knows about the company and the project, and the agent doesn't. The Company Information card has the basic fields: company name and description, version control system and git base URL, git user, CI/CD system, issue tracker, wiki and team messenger. For our task the key ones are GitHub as the VCS and GitHub Actions as CI/CD, because they decide which workflows the agent will write. You don't need to upload documents for a new project yet: there's nothing to describe. On a live project, this is where you put what usually sits in the wiki and in people's heads: the network diagram, naming conventions, where state lives, what's special about each environment. You can upload a Markdown document or ask the agent to generate one from a list of repositories. When a plan finishes, nib writes a report and updates the knowledge base from it, so the next task starts with what the agent learned in the previous one. Connecting GitHub, AWS and search over MCP On its own, the agent can only think. To create a repository, look at AWS resources or find documentation, it needs tools. In nib they connect over MCP (Model Context Protocol). It's an open protocol: an LLM application gets a list of tools from an external server and calls them. One MCP server covers one system: GitHub, AWS, search. If you don't know where to start, ask nib itself, for example: "How do I connect you to AWS over MCP?" Its answer is in the video. This task needs three servers: GitHub : the repository, PRs and workflows; AWS : reading and creating resources in the account; SearXNG : web search, so the agent can check current documentation instead of relying only on what the model already knows. nib supports only the HTTP transport for MCP (streamable HTTP), so we run all three servers as containers on the same network as nib. Add them to docker-compose.yml . GitHub MCP is the official server from GitHub: github-mcp : image : ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server:latest restart : unless-stopped command : - http - --port=9082 networks : - nib aws-mcp : image : public.ecr.aws/awslabs-mcp/awslabs/aws-api-mcp-server:latest restart : unless-stopped environment : AWS_API_MCP_TRANSPORT : " streamable-http" AWS_API_MCP_HOST : " 0.0.0.0" AWS_API_MCP_PORT : " 9081" AUTH_TYPE : " no-auth" AWS_REGION : " ${AWS_REGION:-us-east-2}" AWS_API_MCP_ALLOWED_HOSTS : " aws-mcp,localhost,127.0.0.1" AWS_API_MCP_ALLOWED_ORIGINS : " aws-mcp,localhost,127.0.0.1" READ_OPERATIONS_ONLY : " false" REQUIRE_MUTATION_CONSENT : " false" AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID : " ${AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID}" AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY : " ${AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY}" AWS_SESSION_TOKEN : " ${AWS_SESSION_TOKEN:-}" networks : - nib searxng : image : docker.io/searxng/searxng:latest restart : unless-stopped environment : SEARXNG_PORT : " 9083" SEARXNG_BASE_URL : " http://searxng:9083/" SEARXNG_SECRET : " ${SEARXNG_SECRET}" volumes : - ./searxng:/etc/searxng:rw networks : - nib searxng-mcp : image : docker.io/isokoliuk/mcp-searxng:latest restart : unless-stopped environment : SEARXNG_URL : " http://searxng:9083" SEARXNG_DEFAULT_RESPONSE_FORMAT : " json" SEARXNG_MAX_RESULT_CHARS : " 500" SEARXNG_TIMEOUT_MS : " 15000" MCP_HTTP_PORT : " 9084" MCP_HTTP_HOST : " 0.0.0.0" MCP_HTTP_STATELESS : " true" networks : - nib The response format is an easy place to trip up. The MCP wrapper asks SearXNG for results in JSON, but by default SearXNG returns only HTML. The json format has to be enabled in searxng/settings.yml . The nib repository already ships this file with the right setting, which is why the volume is mounted from ./searxng . Registering the servers in nib Now nib needs to know where to find these servers. You edit the MCP config in Tools → Config (or through Tools → MCP Servers → Add ): { "mcpServers" : { "knowledge-base" : { "url" : "http://kb-mcp:8081/mcp" }, "aws" : { "type" : "http" , "url" : "http://aws-mcp:9081/mcp" }, "searxng" : { "type" : "http" , "url" : "http://searxng-mcp:9084/mcp" }, "github" : { "type" : "http" , "url" : "http://github-mcp:9082/" , "headers" : { "Authorization" : "Bearer ${GITHUB_TOKEN}" , "X-MCP-Toolsets" : "all" , "X-MCP-Readonly" : "false" } } } } knowledge-base is the built-in knowledge base server, and it's already in the config after installation. We add the other three. Note the ${GITHUB_TOKEN} in the header. Tokens never go into the config as plain text: nib fills them in from Variables → Secrets at request time. Each secret has a list of allowed hosts, so the GitHub token goes only to github-mcp and nowhere else. So secrets live in two places, and it's easy to mix them up: AWS keys are needed by the aws-mcp container itself, so they're in .env and reach the container as environment variables; the GitHub token travels in the HTTP header of the request from nib to the MCP server, so it's in nib's secrets. Checking the connection After restarting the containers, open Tools → MCP Servers . For each server you can see the list of tools it exposes. If the list is empty or the server shows an error, the problem is in the network, the address or the token, and there's no point going further: an agent without tools plans blind. In the video, the very first check fails: GitHub MCP returns an error. The container is up and the address is right, but the GITHUB_TOKEN secret doesn't exist yet, and without it the server returns nothing. We create the secret in Variables → Secrets , check again, and the tool list appears. You create the token in your GitHub user settings, under Developer settings ( github.com/settings/tokens ). I used a classic token with the repo and workflow scopes. The second one is easy to miss: without it GitHub rejects pushes to .github/workflows/ , and the agent can't commit its workflows. In my case GitHub exposed a couple of dozen tools, SearXNG five, and AWS only two. That's expected. AWS API MCP Server gives the agent a generic AWS CLI call plus a helper that picks the right command, so all of AWS fits into two tools. GitHub is the opposite, with one tool per operation, and the next section deals with that. Tool categories and a base set per mode Three MCP servers give the agent a lot of tools. If you send all of them with every call, the model gets confused, the context grows, and you pay tokens for descriptions of tools this task will never use. Planning cloud resources doesn't need tools for logs and metrics. nib has two mechanisms for this. Tool categories. Tools are grouped into categories (for example, everything about AWS, everything about git). During decomposition the agent decides which categories the task touches and gets access only to those. Each action in the plan gets an even narrower set: only the categories marked on that action. You don't have to sort the tools by hand. The Auto-fill with AI button on the Tool categories card does a first pass that you can then fix. A base set for each mode. You can think of nib's modes as subagents: some break the task down, some work out the stages, some run actions. By default every mode gets every tool. In Tools → Included tools you can narrow this: modes that should only read and plan don't need tools that change things. The Distribute with AI button can only remove tools, so the read-only modes lose the tools that change things, and nothing extra gets added. The first plan Everything is ready, so we can plan. As a reminder, we're deploying demo-app , an online store for art supplies with a Python backend, a React frontend and a PostgreSQL database. Click New plan and paste the task from Part 1 as is. From here, nib repeats what the engineer did in Part 1. Collecting context. First the decompose agent asks clarifying questions, and for most of them it suggests answers you can pick with a click. It asked me two questions an engineer would ask whoever filed the ticket in the first five minutes: How should the service be published? Is there a custom domain, or is the address that CloudFront generates enough? The answer decides whether DNS records and a TLS certificate show up in the plan. How should the jobs run? Automatically on merge to the main branch, or manually? Really, this is a question about whether the infrastructure can change without a human. I don't have a domain, so the site lives on the CloudFront address, and the jobs run automatically. Stages and dependencies. After the answers, the agent shows a Summary (how it understood the task) and a DAG of the stages and the dependencies between them. A DAG (directed acyclic graph) is a "what comes after what" diagram with no loops. Here you see for the first time what was implicit in the engineer's head: which stages can run in parallel and which ones block the rest. If you have no questions about the stages, move on to detailed planning. Actions, checks, rollback. The Process plan here button starts planning. A separate agent works on each stage, in parallel with the others, and at the end the rollback plan is built. The whole thing took about two minutes. The result was four stages and a rollback plan: Look at the last row: there are one and a half times more checks than actions. When the plan lives in your head, this is the part that shrinks first under a deadline. Steps come in four types: run a CLI command, make an API request, work with code, or change something in a web UI. Each step has a detailed description of what to do, and if an action can cause downtime for a system that's already running, the plan warns about it separately. This answers the third problem from Part 1. nib doesn't estimate in hours, but you see the amount of work before you start: four stages, ten steps, fifteen checks, and it's clear where you need code and where an API call is enough. You can take that to whoever asked "how long will it take," and the conversation will be more concrete than "a day or two." Preparing access: the agent works over MCP Each step has a run button, each stage has Execute all , and you can also start a step from the chat by asking the agent. A checkbox next to a step marks it as done, and you can leave a comment on any step. Only one action runs at a time. This is a deliberate limit, so that two agents don't change the same infrastructure in parallel. The first stage is all API and CLI calls, so the agent ran it on its own, over MCP: Reconcile the GitHub Actions OIDC provider in AWS account : the OIDC provider that GitHub Actions will use to get access to AWS; Reconcile the remote Terraform state bucket for the prod stack : an S3 bucket for the Terraform state; Reconcile the infrastructure deployment role used by Terraform : the role Terraform uses to create resources; Reconcile the application deployment role for publishing and rolling out : a separate role for shipping the application; Create or reconcile the protected GitHub production environment : a protected production environment in the repository. If you know Kubernetes, you know the word reconcile: bring the system to the desired state. If the resource doesn't exist, create it. If it exists but is configured differently, fix it. If it's already right, do nothing. A step like this is safe to run again, which helps if the plan stops halfway. The two separate roles are deliberate too: the role that ships the application has no reason to be able to create networks and databases. After each step, the agent reports in the chat what it did. To make the demo clearer, I ran the stage checks myself: I opened the AWS console and made sure the OIDC provider was created, the bucket was there, and the environment had appeared in the repository. The agent can run the checks too; you just have to ask. Remember the OIDC provider check. We'll need it later. Code: Terraform and workflows In the second stage, API calls are no longer enough: we need to write Terraform and workflows. For steps like these, nib has an executor that runs a coding agent in a separate container. The agent clones the repository, makes the changes, commits, pushes and opens a pull request. The first time you run a code step, nib sends you to the executor settings page ( Tools → Executor ). The executor has three options: off (the default), Local , which means containers on your machine through Docker, and Remote , which runs as Kubernetes Jobs. Local is enough to start: the agent runs right on your computer, and you can see the container logs in the UI. Pick the agent type and the authentication method. The tokens we need aren't in the secrets list yet, so we create them: CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN : the Claude Code subscription token, which you get from claude setup-token . You can use an Anthropic API key instead; a GitHub token, so the agent can push its changes. It's the same one as for MCP. You can keep the default agent image and model. Go back to the plan and run the step. What the agent wrote The PR has 20 files: two workflows, Terraform code in infra/terraform and an updated README. In short, here's the architecture: CloudFront in front of everything: the frontend's static files come from a private S3 bucket, and /api/* requests go to an ALB ; the ALB accepts traffic only from the CloudFront managed prefix list, so you can't reach it directly from the internet; the backend runs on ECS Fargate in private subnets and accepts traffic only from the ALB; RDS PostgreSQL 16 sits in isolated subnets with no route to the internet. It's Multi-AZ, encrypted, with backups and deletion protection. Terraform generates the password and puts it straight into Secrets Manager ; GitHub Actions reach AWS over OIDC : the job assumes an IAM role and gets temporary credentials, so not a single long-lived AWS key is stored in GitHub. This is where the provider and the roles from the first stage come in. And two workflows: Deploy Infrastructure runs terraform plan and terraform apply . Apply runs only manually, with an explicit flag, in the production GitHub environment, where you can require approval. That's how the agent used my answer about running jobs; Deploy Application builds the backend image, pushes it to ECR tagged with the commit, updates the ECS service, builds the frontend, uploads it to S3, invalidates the CloudFront cache and finally runs a smoke test against the CloudFront address. Two decisions in this code are good examples of the "experience" from Part 1 that usually isn't written down anywhere. The ECS service is created with desired_count = 0 . When terraform apply runs, ECR doesn't have a single application image yet. If you ask for two tasks right away, ECS will keep trying to start an image that doesn't exist. So Terraform creates the service empty and ignores later changes to the image and the task count, and the deploy workflow publishes the first real image and scales the service to two. Without this detail, Terraform would undo the deploy on every run. The cost is stated openly. A Multi-AZ database and a NAT gateway in every availability zone are a production setup, and they cost money even with no traffic. The agent put this in the README, next to the order in which to run the workflows. For a demo it's overkill, for production it's right, and it's a decision you should make on purpose instead of learning about it from the bill. The changes look reasonable, so we merge the PR into the main branch. First run, first failure We run Deploy Infrastructure , and the first attempt fails. This happens to experienced engineers too, so it's no big deal. Instead of reading the log myself, I show nib the error and ask it to figure it out. It finds the cause: the OIDC provider created in the first stage doesn't list all the thumbprints. A thumbprint is a fingerprint of the identity provider's TLS certificate. AWS uses the list of thumbprints to verify that the token really came from GitHub. If the right thumbprint isn't on the list, AWS doesn't trust the token, and the job can't assume the role and get into the account. We add the missing thumbprints and rerun the workflow. On the second try the infrastructure is created: the log shows the terraform plan and how many resources were created. We check that the database is ready and the load balancer is in place, and mark the steps as done. Deploying the app: a second failure, then the site We run Deploy Application , and it also fails the first time: the healthcheck doesn't pass. The deploy finished too quickly, and the app wasn't ready by the time of the check. This is expected, and the next step of the plan says exactly that: rerun the deploy. So we do. On the second run the deploy passes and the smoke test is green. We open the CloudFront address and see the art-supply store, the service we set out to deploy. We mark the remaining steps and click Finish . nib closes the plan, writes a report on the work done and updates the knowledge base. Next time a task about this project comes in, the agent will already know that it has a VPC, an ECS cluster and a database, and won't start from zero. Wrapping up We took an ordinary task: deploy a web service to AWS and set up GitHub jobs to deploy it. In two minutes nib split it into four stages with ten steps, fifteen checks and a rollback plan. The agent prepared AWS and GitHub access on its own over MCP, the executor wrote the Terraform and the workflows, and we worked through two failures on the way, the OIDC provider and the healthcheck, together with nib. At the end we opened the site and saw the store working. Back to the three problems from Part 1: Items don't get lost. The action list is written down in the plan. You can see it, hand it to a colleague and pick up where you left off. Checks don't get skipped. They're written into every stage in advance, and the agent isn't tempted to save time on them. Still, the OIDC story showed that a check is only as useful as it is precise. The size is visible before you start. You know how many stages and steps are ahead before the first command runs. The decisions stay with you: you choose which steps to run, you read the PR, and you accept the result. Even if you don't plan to use agents, try writing the plan for your next task in three columns: action, check, rollback. That alone solves the first problem and makes the second one much easier. In Part 1 I said that an engineer relies on team rules and their own experience. You can give nib the same things. In the next post I'll show how to connect your own rules, skills and knowledge base, so the plans come out more accurate and closer to how your team works. The repository is here: github.com/javdet/nib . Try it on a task of your own, and tell me in the comments: which infrastructure task would you trust to an agent first, and which one never?

Inside that line are a network, containers, a database, secrets, a CDN, two workflows and dozens of small steps that an engineer usually keeps in their head. That works while nothing interrupts you. Then the engineer walks the whole list: action, check, action, check. If a check fails, they roll back or fix the problem, and check again.
