Now let's run the same task through nib. The whole run is on video:

What you need
  • Docker;
  • an API key for an LLM provider. nib works with any OpenAI-compatible API, and the installer has presets for OpenAI, OpenRouter, Google Gemini, Qwen, DeepSeek, Grok and Kimi;
  • an AWS account. I strongly recommend a separate sandbox account: the agent will need keys that can create resources;
  • a GitHub account and a fork of demo-app, if you want to repeat this exact task.
Installation

nib runs locally with Docker Compose or in Kubernetes with a Helm chart. The local option is enough to try it:

git clone https://github.com/javdet/nib.git
cd nib
make setup

make setup is an interactive script. It asks for the LLM provider, the model and the key (I use OpenRouter), then the name of your first project and, optionally, its environments, clouds and regions. You can skip those fields, but nib plans better with them, and you can add more projects later. Then the script generates tokens, writes .env and the config, and starts four containers: Postgres, the knowledge base server, the backend and the frontend.

At the end it prints the UI address (http://localhost:8080 by default; if the port is busy, it picks a free one) and an API token. You paste this token on the login screen. It's also saved in .env as NIB_API_TOKEN, so it's hard to lose.

Knowledge base: what to fill in for a new project

The first place to open after you log in is Knowledgebase. This is the "context" from step 1: everything the engineer knows about the company and the project, and the agent doesn't.

The Company Information card has the basic fields: company name and description, version control system and git base URL, git user, CI/CD system, issue tracker, wiki and team messenger. For our task the key ones are GitHub as the VCS and GitHub Actions as CI/CD, because they decide which workflows the agent will write.


You don't need to upload documents for a new project yet: there's nothing to describe. On a live project, this is where you put what usually sits in the wiki and in people's heads: the network diagram, naming conventions, where state lives, what's special about each environment. You can upload a Markdown document or ask the agent to generate one from a list of repositories.

When a plan finishes, nib writes a report and updates the knowledge base from it, so the next task starts with what the agent learned in the previous one.

Connecting GitHub, AWS and search over MCP

On its own, the agent can only think. To create a repository, look at AWS resources or find documentation, it needs tools. In nib they connect over MCP (Model Context Protocol). It's an open protocol: an LLM application gets a list of tools from an external server and calls them. One MCP server covers one system: GitHub, AWS, search.

If you don't know where to start, ask nib itself, for example: "How do I connect you to AWS over MCP?" Its answer is in the video.
This task needs three servers:

  • GitHub: the repository, PRs and workflows;
  • AWS: reading and creating resources in the account;
  • SearXNG: web search, so the agent can check current documentation instead of relying only on what the model already knows.

nib supports only the HTTP transport for MCP (streamable HTTP), so we run all three servers as containers on the same network as nib. Add them to docker-compose.yml.

GitHub MCP is the official server from GitHub:

github-mcp:
  image: ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server:latest
  restart: unless-stopped
  command:
    - http
    - --port=9082
  networks:
    - nib
aws-mcp:
  image: public.ecr.aws/awslabs-mcp/awslabs/aws-api-mcp-server:latest
  restart: unless-stopped
  environment:
    AWS_API_MCP_TRANSPORT: "streamable-http"
    AWS_API_MCP_HOST: "0.0.0.0"
    AWS_API_MCP_PORT: "9081"
    AUTH_TYPE: "no-auth"
    AWS_REGION: "${AWS_REGION:-us-east-2}"
    AWS_API_MCP_ALLOWED_HOSTS: "aws-mcp,localhost,127.0.0.1"
    AWS_API_MCP_ALLOWED_ORIGINS: "aws-mcp,localhost,127.0.0.1"
    READ_OPERATIONS_ONLY: "false"
    REQUIRE_MUTATION_CONSENT: "false"
    AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: "${AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID}"
    AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: "${AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY}"
    AWS_SESSION_TOKEN: "${AWS_SESSION_TOKEN:-}"
  networks:
    - nib
searxng:
  image: docker.io/searxng/searxng:latest
  restart: unless-stopped
  environment:
    SEARXNG_PORT: "9083"
    SEARXNG_BASE_URL: "http://searxng:9083/"
    SEARXNG_SECRET: "${SEARXNG_SECRET}"
  volumes:
    - ./searxng:/etc/searxng:rw
  networks:
    - nib

searxng-mcp:
  image: docker.io/isokoliuk/mcp-searxng:latest
  restart: unless-stopped
  environment:
    SEARXNG_URL: "http://searxng:9083"
    SEARXNG_DEFAULT_RESPONSE_FORMAT: "json"
    SEARXNG_MAX_RESULT_CHARS: "500"
    SEARXNG_TIMEOUT_MS: "15000"
    MCP_HTTP_PORT: "9084"
    MCP_HTTP_HOST: "0.0.0.0"
    MCP_HTTP_STATELESS: "true"
  networks:
    - nib

The response format is an easy place to trip up. The MCP wrapper asks SearXNG for results in JSON, but by default SearXNG returns only HTML. The json format has to be enabled in searxng/settings.yml. The nib repository already ships this file with the right setting, which is why the volume is mounted from ./searxng.

Registering the servers in nib

Now nib needs to know where to find these servers. You edit the MCP config in Tools → Config (or through Tools → MCP Servers → Add):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "knowledge-base": {
      "url": "http://kb-mcp:8081/mcp"
    },
    "aws": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "http://aws-mcp:9081/mcp"
    },
    "searxng": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "http://searxng-mcp:9084/mcp"
    },
    "github": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "http://github-mcp:9082/",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer ${GITHUB_TOKEN}",
        "X-MCP-Toolsets": "all",
        "X-MCP-Readonly": "false"
      }
    }
  }
}


knowledge-base is the built-in knowledge base server, and it's already in the config after installation. We add the other three.

Note the ${GITHUB_TOKEN} in the header. Tokens never go into the config as plain text: nib fills them in from Variables → Secrets at request time. Each secret has a list of allowed hosts, so the GitHub token goes only to github-mcp and nowhere else.

So secrets live in two places, and it's easy to mix them up:

  • AWS keys are needed by the aws-mcp container itself, so they're in .env and reach the container as environment variables;
  • the GitHub token travels in the HTTP header of the request from nib to the MCP server, so it's in nib's secrets.
Checking the connection

After restarting the containers, open Tools → MCP Servers. For each server you can see the list of tools it exposes. If the list is empty or the server shows an error, the problem is in the network, the address or the token, and there's no point going further: an agent without tools plans blind.

In the video, the very first check fails: GitHub MCP returns an error. The container is up and the address is right, but the GITHUB_TOKEN secret doesn't exist yet, and without it the server returns nothing. We create the secret in Variables → Secrets, check again, and the tool list appears.

You create the token in your GitHub user settings, under Developer settings (github.com/settings/tokens). I used a classic token with the repo and workflow scopes. The second one is easy to miss: without it GitHub rejects pushes to .github/workflows/, and the agent can't commit its workflows.
In my case GitHub exposed a couple of dozen tools, SearXNG five, and AWS only two. That's expected. AWS API MCP Server gives the agent a generic AWS CLI call plus a helper that picks the right command, so all of AWS fits into two tools. GitHub is the opposite, with one tool per operation, and the next section deals with that.

Tool categories and a base set per mode

Three MCP servers give the agent a lot of tools. If you send all of them with every call, the model gets confused, the context grows, and you pay tokens for descriptions of tools this task will never use. Planning cloud resources doesn't need tools for logs and metrics. nib has two mechanisms for this.

Tool categories. Tools are grouped into categories (for example, everything about AWS, everything about git). During decomposition the agent decides which categories the task touches and gets access only to those. Each action in the plan gets an even narrower set: only the categories marked on that action. You don't have to sort the tools by hand. The Auto-fill with AI button on the Tool categories card does a first pass that you can then fix.

A base set for each mode. You can think of nib's modes as subagents: some break the task down, some work out the stages, some run actions. By default every mode gets every tool. In Tools → Included tools you can narrow this: modes that should only read and plan don't need tools that change things. The Distribute with AI button can only remove tools, so the read-only modes lose the tools that change things, and nothing extra gets added.

The first plan

Everything is ready, so we can plan. As a reminder, we're deploying demo-app, an online store for art supplies with a Python backend, a React frontend and a PostgreSQL database. Click New plan and paste the task from Part 1 as is.

From here, nib repeats what the engineer did in Part 1.

Collecting context. First the decompose agent asks clarifying questions, and for most of them it suggests answers you can pick with a click. It asked me two questions an engineer would ask whoever filed the ticket in the first five minutes:

  • How should the service be published? Is there a custom domain, or is the address that CloudFront generates enough? The answer decides whether DNS records and a TLS certificate show up in the plan.
  • How should the jobs run? Automatically on merge to the main branch, or manually? Really, this is a question about whether the infrastructure can change without a human.

I don't have a domain, so the site lives on the CloudFront address, and the jobs run automatically.


Stages and dependencies. After the answers, the agent shows a Summary (how it understood the task) and a DAG of the stages and the dependencies between them. A DAG (directed acyclic graph) is a "what comes after what" diagram with no loops. Here you see for the first time what was implicit in the engineer's head: which stages can run in parallel and which ones block the rest. If you have no questions about the stages, move on to detailed planning.


Actions, checks, rollback. The Process plan here button starts planning. A separate agent works on each stage, in parallel with the others, and at the end the rollback plan is built. The whole thing took about two minutes. The result was four stages and a rollback plan:


Look at the last row: there are one and a half times more checks than actions. When the plan lives in your head, this is the part that shrinks first under a deadline.

Steps come in four types: run a CLI command, make an API request, work with code, or change something in a web UI. Each step has a detailed description of what to do, and if an action can cause downtime for a system that's already running, the plan warns about it separately.


This answers the third problem from Part 1. nib doesn't estimate in hours, but you see the amount of work before you start: four stages, ten steps, fifteen checks, and it's clear where you need code and where an API call is enough. You can take that to whoever asked "how long will it take," and the conversation will be more concrete than "a day or two."

Preparing access: the agent works over MCP

Each step has a run button, each stage has Execute all, and you can also start a step from the chat by asking the agent. A checkbox next to a step marks it as done, and you can leave a comment on any step. Only one action runs at a time. This is a deliberate limit, so that two agents don't change the same infrastructure in parallel.

The first stage is all API and CLI calls, so the agent ran it on its own, over MCP:

  1. Reconcile the GitHub Actions OIDC provider in AWS account: the OIDC provider that GitHub Actions will use to get access to AWS;
  2. Reconcile the remote Terraform state bucket for the prod stack: an S3 bucket for the Terraform state;
  3. Reconcile the infrastructure deployment role used by Terraform: the role Terraform uses to create resources;
  4. Reconcile the application deployment role for publishing and rolling out: a separate role for shipping the application;
  5. Create or reconcile the protected GitHub production environment: a protected production environment in the repository.

If you know Kubernetes, you know the word reconcile: bring the system to the desired state. If the resource doesn't exist, create it. If it exists but is configured differently, fix it. If it's already right, do nothing. A step like this is safe to run again, which helps if the plan stops halfway. The two separate roles are deliberate too: the role that ships the application has no reason to be able to create networks and databases.

After each step, the agent reports in the chat what it did. To make the demo clearer, I ran the stage checks myself: I opened the AWS console and made sure the OIDC provider was created, the bucket was there, and the environment had appeared in the repository. The agent can run the checks too; you just have to ask. Remember the OIDC provider check. We'll need it later.

Code: Terraform and workflows

In the second stage, API calls are no longer enough: we need to write Terraform and workflows. For steps like these, nib has an executor that runs a coding agent in a separate container. The agent clones the repository, makes the changes, commits, pushes and opens a pull request.

The first time you run a code step, nib sends you to the executor settings page (Tools → Executor). The executor has three options: off (the default), Local, which means containers on your machine through Docker, and Remote, which runs as Kubernetes Jobs. Local is enough to start: the agent runs right on your computer, and you can see the container logs in the UI.

Pick the agent type and the authentication method. The tokens we need aren't in the secrets list yet, so we create them:

  • CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN: the Claude Code subscription token, which you get from claude setup-token. You can use an Anthropic API key instead;
  • a GitHub token, so the agent can push its changes. It's the same one as for MCP.

You can keep the default agent image and model. Go back to the plan and run the step.

What the agent wrote

The PR has 20 files: two workflows, Terraform code in infra/terraform and an updated README. In short, here's the architecture:

  • CloudFront in front of everything: the frontend's static files come from a private S3 bucket, and /api/* requests go to an ALB;
  • the ALB accepts traffic only from the CloudFront managed prefix list, so you can't reach it directly from the internet;
  • the backend runs on ECS Fargate in private subnets and accepts traffic only from the ALB;
  • RDS PostgreSQL 16 sits in isolated subnets with no route to the internet. It's Multi-AZ, encrypted, with backups and deletion protection. Terraform generates the password and puts it straight into Secrets Manager;
  • GitHub Actions reach AWS over OIDC: the job assumes an IAM role and gets temporary credentials, so not a single long-lived AWS key is stored in GitHub. This is where the provider and the roles from the first stage come in.

And two workflows:

  • Deploy Infrastructure runs terraform plan and terraform apply. Apply runs only manually, with an explicit flag, in the production GitHub environment, where you can require approval. That's how the agent used my answer about running jobs;
  • Deploy Application builds the backend image, pushes it to ECR tagged with the commit, updates the ECS service, builds the frontend, uploads it to S3, invalidates the CloudFront cache and finally runs a smoke test against the CloudFront address.

Two decisions in this code are good examples of the "experience" from Part 1 that usually isn't written down anywhere.

The ECS service is created with desired_count = 0. When terraform apply runs, ECR doesn't have a single application image yet. If you ask for two tasks right away, ECS will keep trying to start an image that doesn't exist. So Terraform creates the service empty and ignores later changes to the image and the task count, and the deploy workflow publishes the first real image and scales the service to two. Without this detail, Terraform would undo the deploy on every run.

The cost is stated openly. A Multi-AZ database and a NAT gateway in every availability zone are a production setup, and they cost money even with no traffic. The agent put this in the README, next to the order in which to run the workflows. For a demo it's overkill, for production it's right, and it's a decision you should make on purpose instead of learning about it from the bill.

The changes look reasonable, so we merge the PR into the main branch.

First run, first failure

We run Deploy Infrastructure, and the first attempt fails.


This happens to experienced engineers too, so it's no big deal. Instead of reading the log myself, I show nib the error and ask it to figure it out. It finds the cause: the OIDC provider created in the first stage doesn't list all the thumbprints.

A thumbprint is a fingerprint of the identity provider's TLS certificate. AWS uses the list of thumbprints to verify that the token really came from GitHub. If the right thumbprint isn't on the list, AWS doesn't trust the token, and the job can't assume the role and get into the account.


We add the missing thumbprints and rerun the workflow. On the second try the infrastructure is created: the log shows the terraform plan and how many resources were created. We check that the database is ready and the load balancer is in place, and mark the steps as done.

Deploying the app: a second failure, then the site

We run Deploy Application, and it also fails the first time: the healthcheck doesn't pass. The deploy finished too quickly, and the app wasn't ready by the time of the check. This is expected, and the next step of the plan says exactly that: rerun the deploy. So we do.


On the second run the deploy passes and the smoke test is green. We open the CloudFront address and see the art-supply store, the service we set out to deploy.


We mark the remaining steps and click Finish. nib closes the plan, writes a report on the work done and updates the knowledge base. Next time a task about this project comes in, the agent will already know that it has a VPC, an ECS cluster and a database, and won't start from zero.

Wrapping up

We took an ordinary task: deploy a web service to AWS and set up GitHub jobs to deploy it. In two minutes nib split it into four stages with ten steps, fifteen checks and a rollback plan. The agent prepared AWS and GitHub access on its own over MCP, the executor wrote the Terraform and the workflows, and we worked through two failures on the way, the OIDC provider and the healthcheck, together with nib. At the end we opened the site and saw the store working.

Back to the three problems from Part 1:

  • Items don't get lost. The action list is written down in the plan. You can see it, hand it to a colleague and pick up where you left off.
  • Checks don't get skipped. They're written into every stage in advance, and the agent isn't tempted to save time on them. Still, the OIDC story showed that a check is only as useful as it is precise.
  • The size is visible before you start. You know how many stages and steps are ahead before the first command runs.

The decisions stay with you: you choose which steps to run, you read the PR, and you accept the result.

Even if you don't plan to use agents, try writing the plan for your next task in three columns: action, check, rollback. That alone solves the first problem and makes the second one much easier.

In Part 1 I said that an engineer relies on team rules and their own experience. You can give nib the same things. In the next post I'll show how to connect your own rules, skills and knowledge base, so the plans come out more accurate and closer to how your team works.

The repository is here: github.com/javdet/nib. Try it on a task of your own, and tell me in the comments: which infrastructure task would you trust to an agent first, and which one never?

items.title: Free AI blocks for any static site: copy, paste, it works (no backend)
items.summary: I run a few static sites (GitHub Pages, a couple of single HTML files) and every time I wanted an AI feature on one of them, the answer was "add a backend". So I made twelve blocks that don't need one. Static AI Block is a gallery of copy-paste blocks: ask this page, summarize, translate, FAQ bot, draft a reply, rewrite, extract to JSON, smart search, alt text for images, a quiz from the page, and an Explain button for code. Each block is plain HTML and vanilla JavaScript, 40–60 lines, no framework, no build step. Live gallery (every block runs right there): https://aiblock.onetagai.com/?ref=devto Repo (MIT): https://github.com/fengyiqicoder/static-ai-block How it works: the block loads one script tag from OneTag AI and calls onetag.ask(prompt, input) from the browser. input can be a string, any element on the page, a form, an image or a plain object; the answer streams back, or comes back as JSON with json: true . The key is public by design, like an analytics ID; it can only spend that account's free allowance (1,000,000 tokens). You get one by posting your email: curl -X POST https://onetagai.com/api/signup -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"email":"you@example.com"}' Two things I tried to get right: Each block says what it does in one line and has an example you can click. No reading required. "Copy to AI" copies the block together with the setup steps, so you can paste it into Cursor or Claude Code and let the agent sign you up and wire it in. What I'd like to hear: which block you'd actually put on a page, and which one is missing. The list is MIT, so PRs with new blocks are welcome; a block is one HTML file with a comment on the first line.
items.summary_html:
I run a few static sites (GitHub Pages, a couple of single HTML files) and every time I wanted an AI feature on one of them, the answer was "add a backend". So I made twelve blocks that don't need one.

Static AI Block is a gallery of copy-paste blocks: ask this page, summarize, translate, FAQ bot, draft a reply, rewrite, extract to JSON, smart search, alt text for images, a quiz from the page, and an Explain button for code. Each block is plain HTML and vanilla JavaScript, 40–60 lines, no framework, no build step.

Live gallery (every block runs right there): https://aiblock.onetagai.com/?ref=devto
Repo (MIT): https://github.com/fengyiqicoder/static-ai-block

How it works: the block loads one script tag from OneTag AI and calls onetag.ask(prompt, input) from the browser. input can be a string, any element on the page, a form, an image or a plain object; the answer streams back, or comes back as JSON with json: true. The key is public by design, like an analytics ID; it can only spend that account's free allowance (1,000,000 tokens). You get one by posting your email:

curl -X POST https://onetagai.com/api/signup -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"email":"you@example.com"}'

Two things I tried to get right:

  1. Each block says what it does in one line and has an example you can click. No reading required.
  2. "Copy to AI" copies the block together with the setup steps, so you can paste it into Cursor or Claude Code and let the agent sign you up and wire it in.

What I'd like to hear: which block you'd actually put on a page, and which one is missing. The list is MIT, so PRs with new blocks are welcome; a block is one HTML file with a comment on the first line.

items.title: Your Agent Is Only as Good as Your Codebase
items.summary: Picture an agent fixing a bug in one place. The same logic lives in two other files. It doesn't know, so it doesn't touch them, and the bug stays alive in two out of three code paths. That's not the agent being dumb. It read the file I pointed at, found the logic, fixed it, and ran the tests. The tests passed because nothing tested the other two copies. The codebase lied to it, and it believed the codebase. That's the whole argument of this post. Agents copy what they find. Give them a clean repo and they write clean code. Give them a tangled one and they write more tangle, faster than you ever could. Why structure changes what an agent writes A human who has lived in a repo for a year carries a map in their head. They know the tax logic is copied in checkout/ and invoices/ . They know you have to call init() before load() . An agent starts every session without that map. It only has what it can read. So every hidden link in your code turns into a trap: Duplicated logic means the agent fixes one copy and ships. A call order callers just have to know means it calls them in the wrong order, and nothing tells it. An if for one special value looks like a pattern, so the agent adds a second one next to it for the next special value. A module with no tests means the agent can change its behaviour and stay green. It costs more, too. Not in money, in context. When one change has to land in five files, the agent has to find all five, read them, and keep them in its head at once. When the change lands in one place, it reads one file. Less to read means less to get wrong, and more room left in the context window for the actual task. Fixing the codebase is the cheapest way to make an agent better. Better prompts won't fix a repo that hides its own rules. items.summary_html:
Picture an agent fixing a bug in one place. The same logic lives in two other files. It doesn't know, so it doesn't touch them, and the bug stays alive in two out of three code paths.

That's not the agent being dumb. It read the file I pointed at, found the logic, fixed it, and ran the tests. The tests passed because nothing tested the other two copies. The codebase lied to it, and it believed the codebase.

That's the whole argument of this post. Agents copy what they find. Give them a clean repo and they write clean code. Give them a tangled one and they write more tangle, faster than you ever could.

Why structure changes what an agent writes

A human who has lived in a repo for a year carries a map in their head. They know the tax logic is copied in checkout/ and invoices/. They know you have to call init() before load(). An agent starts every session without that map. It only has what it can read.

So every hidden link in your code turns into a trap:

  • Duplicated logic means the agent fixes one copy and ships.
  • A call order callers just have to know means it calls them in the wrong order, and nothing tells it.
  • An if for one special value looks like a pattern, so the agent adds a second one next to it for the next special value.
  • A module with no tests means the agent can change its behaviour and stay green.

It costs more, too. Not in money, in context. When one change has to land in five files, the agent has to find all five, read them, and keep them in its head at once. When the change lands in one place, it reads one file. Less to read means less to get wrong, and more room left in the context window for the actual task.

Fixing the codebase is the cheapest way to make an agent better. Better prompts won't fix a repo that hides its own rules.

What dev-refactor does

RayStack 1.3.0 ships a new skill called dev-refactor. You run it with /raystack project refactor, or the new short alias /rs refactor. It refactors a whole repo, or one area of it, without changing what the code does. The order never changes.

1. It asks two things. Scope first: the whole repo or one folder (it offers the folders it found). Then two optional extras: strip comments that only restate the code, and remove tests that can't catch a bug.

2. It names the architecture you already have. MVC, layered, hexagonal, feature folders, framework default. It writes down the pattern and the evidence, then refactors inside it. If the pattern itself is the problem, it says so and points you to dev-migrate. Switching architecture is a different job, and it won't sneak one in.

3. Safety net before any change. It finds the test runner, runs the whole suite, and records the result as a baseline. A red baseline stops the run and asks you what to do. Then, for every module it plans to touch that has no tests, it writes characterisation tests that pin today's behaviour, odd cases and errors included. Those go in their own commit, before a single line of refactor.

4. It lists every problem, and changes nothing yet. The list goes to docs/refactor/YYYY-MM-DD-log.md, one line per problem with file:line. It looks for hidden links, needless links (callers poking at internals, shallow wrappers), surplus code, and special cases. DRY counts only when the copies change for the same reason. Two lookalikes that change for different reasons stay apart. SOLID counts as far as it pays: no interface with one implementation, no extension point nobody uses.

5. Redesign. It works out the fixes as if today's requirements had been known from day one, and writes each fix above the problems it solves. One good fix usually kills three or four lines of the list.

6. Small commits. One fix group per commit, suite green after each. A red run gets fixed or reverted before the next step. It never weakens a test, raises a timeout, or adds a suppression to get green.

7. A fresh reviewer. A new read-only subagent gets the log, the diff and the problem lenses, and hunts for what's left. Real findings get fixed, then another fresh reviewer goes again. It stops when the reviewer finds nothing worth fixing.

8. Ship. PR, self-review, green CI, merge. The log records the PR and the before and after counts.

The change-together idea in step 4 (copies only count as duplication when they change for the same reason) comes from caldoai's untangle-codebase skill, which is MIT licensed. It's the rule that stops DRY from turning into a pile of shared helpers nobody can change safely.

A small trial, with real numbers

I built a tiny Node repo with a mess planted in it on purpose. Three modules, one test, the usual sins. Then I ran /rs refactor on it.

Measure Before After Special cases (an if on one value) 10 1 Duplicated blocks 3 0 Modules without tests 2 of 3 0 of 4 Tests 1 28

Old and new code gave identical output on 132,022 generated inputs.

The interesting part was the first reviewer. It caught a behaviour change that all 28 new tests missed. The old code compared a rule's country with a plain equality check. The refactor normalised it into a list lookup, roughly like this:

// before
if (rule.country === order.country) { /* ... */ }

// after (first pass)
if ([rule.country].flat().includes(order.country)) { /* ... */ }

That's why step 7 exists. Tests you write while refactoring share the blind spots of the person (or agent) doing the refactor. A reviewer that didn't write any of it doesn't.

It also kept one special case on purpose: a single if for the HALF coupon. That's a real business rule, not a missed abstraction. Building a coupon strategy system around one coupon would be the exact surplus step 4 is meant to catch.

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HarunRRayhan/RayStack/main/get.sh | bash

/raystack project refactor

items.title: LLM-as-a-judge: building an AI grader you can actually trust
items.summary_html:
Short answer: An LLM judge works when you've calibrated it against human labels. Without calibration it's noise dressed up as a metric. The rubric is the actual work — the judge model just executes it.

Teams reach for LLM-as-judge because there's no other way to automatically score whether a support reply was "empathetic" or whether a generated SQL query "answers the user's intent." There's no diff to run. The judge fills the gap between "does it parse" (easy to check mechanically) and "is it actually good" (hard to check without a human).

The failure mode is treating it as plug-and-play: pick a model, write a prompt like "rate this output from 1–10," drop it in CI, declare victory. That judge gives you a consistent number that correlates poorly with what users actually think. You've built a metric that feels like signal and isn't.

Here's how to build one that isn't that.

Why do LLM judges fail without calibration?

Three problems, all fixable.

Position bias. In pairwise comparisons, judges prefer whichever answer appears first — consistently enough to flip verdicts up to 30% of the time. A test that scores "response A vs response B" will sometimes return a different result just from swapping the order.

Verbosity preference. Most LLMs, when asked to judge quality without a tight rubric, prefer longer outputs. A wrong-but-detailed answer beats a correct-but-brief one. Your eval suite ends up rewarding word count. Users don't.

Same-model blindness. Claude evaluating Claude's outputs is lenient on its own artifacts. It misses the specific failure modes it produces. If your app uses a model and you judge with the same model, you get a blind spot for exactly the class of errors you need to catch.

What makes a rubric tight enough to trust?

The rubric is not the prompt template. It's the list of concrete criteria the judge checks against. Write it as conditions, not adjectives.

Bad rubric:

Score 1–10 for quality. Consider clarity, accuracy, and helpfulness.

Good rubric:

A good response:
- Directly answers the question asked (not a related question)
- Does not introduce information not present in the provided context
- Uses plain language; no jargon unless the user used it first
- Is under 200 words

Score 0.0 immediately if any of:
- Response says "I don't know" when the context contains the answer
- Response asks a clarifying question instead of answering
- Response repeats the system prompt

Otherwise score 0.0–1.0 against the criteria above.

The hard-failure conditions matter most. They cover cases where you know it's wrong — no rubric ambiguity. Put them first. They short-circuit scoring before interpretation enters.

Here's a complete judge implementation:

import anthropic

RUBRIC = """\
A good response to a customer support question:
- Directly addresses the specific question asked
- Does not introduce facts not present in the provided knowledge base context
- Is under 200 words
- Uses plain language; no jargon unless the user introduced it
- Ends with a concrete next step or resolution

Score 0.0 immediately if any of the following:
- Says "I cannot help with that" when context contains the answer
- Asks a clarifying question instead of answering
- Contradicts information in the context
- Contains a system prompt fragment

Otherwise score 0.0–1.0 based on the criteria above.
Return only a decimal number (e.g., 0.85). No explanation."""

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

def judge_response(user_question: str, kb_context: str, response: str) -> float:
    prompt = f"""User question: {user_question}

Knowledge base context:
{kb_context}

Response to evaluate:
{response}

Rubric:
{RUBRIC}"""

    result = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-haiku-4-5-20251001",
        max_tokens=10,
        temperature=0,                 # deterministic — same input, same score
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
    )
    try:
        return float(result.content[0].text.strip())
    except ValueError:
        return 0.0                     # unparseable output = treat as failure

Two things to notice: temperature=0 for determinism, and the parsing fallback returns 0.0 instead of crashing. A judge that sometimes returns "0.85 (good answer)" instead of "0.85" should fail safe, not silently inflate your scores.

How do you calibrate before shipping to CI?

You need 20–30 examples labeled by a human against your rubric. Not labeled "correct" — labeled against each criterion: does this response satisfy the condition or not?

# calibration.jsonl — one entry per labeled example
# {"question": "...", "context": "...", "response": "...", "human_score": 0.9, "notes": ""}
# {"question": "...", "context": "...", "response": "...", "human_score": 0.1, "notes": "contradicts context in para 2"}

import json

def calibrate_judge(labeled_path: str, threshold: float = 0.2) -> dict:
    with open(labeled_path) as f:
        examples = [json.loads(line) for line in f if line.strip()]

    disagreements = []
    for ex in examples:
        judge_score = judge_response(ex["question"], ex["context"], ex["response"])
        delta = abs(judge_score - ex["human_score"])
        if delta > threshold:
            disagreements.append({
                "question": ex["question"][:80],
                "human": ex["human_score"],
                "judge": judge_score,
                "delta": round(delta, 2),
                "notes": ex.get("notes", ""),
            })

    agreement_rate = 1 - len(disagreements) / len(examples)
    return {
        "agreement_rate": round(agreement_rate, 3),
        "disagreements": disagreements,
        "verdict": "PASS" if agreement_rate >= 0.80 else "RUBRIC NEEDS WORK",
    }

Run this before wiring the judge into CI. If verdict is RUBRIC NEEDS WORK, look at the disagreement list. Almost always, it's not that the judge model is wrong — it's that your rubric doesn't say what you thought it said. Add the failing condition explicitly and re-run.

Eighty percent agreement is the floor, not the goal. Below 80%, the judge is unreliable and your CI metrics will mislead you into thinking quality is stable when it isn't.

How do you handle position bias in pairwise comparisons?

Run each pair twice with the order swapped. If the judge flips its verdict, the difference isn't real — call it a tie.

def pairwise_judge(question: str, response_a: str, response_b: str) -> str:
    """Returns 'A', 'B', or 'TIE'."""

    def score_pair(first: str, second: str) -> str:
        result = client.messages.create(
            model="claude-haiku-4-5-20251001",
            max_tokens=5,
            temperature=0,
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": (
                f"Question: {question}\n\n"
                f"Response 1: {first}\n\n"
                f"Response 2: {second}\n\n"
                "Which response better satisfies the rubric above? "
                "Reply only: 1, 2, or TIE."
            )}],
        )
        return result.content[0].text.strip()

    verdict_ab = score_pair(response_a, response_b)    # A presented as 1, B as 2
    verdict_ba = score_pair(response_b, response_a)    # B presented as 1, A as 2

    # normalize to A/B labels
    winner_ab = "A" if verdict_ab == "1" else ("B" if verdict_ab == "2" else "TIE")
    winner_ba = "A" if verdict_ba == "2" else ("B" if verdict_ba == "1" else "TIE")

    if winner_ab == winner_ba:
        return winner_ab
    return "TIE"   # order-sensitive result = not a real difference

For single-answer scoring — which is what you want in most CI setups — position bias doesn't apply. There's only one answer, and you score it against the rubric directly.

What does LLM-as-judge not solve?

It doesn't tell you if the rubric is right. If you're measuring the wrong thing — if "under 200 words" is in your rubric but users actually want detailed answers — calibration passes and your eval suite silently optimizes for the wrong outcome. No amount of judge engineering fixes that. Review your labeled examples with someone who understands the product intent before locking the rubric.

It also shouldn't replace mechanical verification. If your LLM writes SQL, run it against a test database. If it writes code, execute it. Use a judge for genuinely subjective dimensions only — the ones where there's no ground truth to diff against. Applying a judge to things you can verify deterministically wastes money and adds noise.

The free test lab has a complete judge harness with calibration script, a 25-example labeled dataset for a support-reply task, and a CI integration that fails the build when judge agreement drops below 80% after a model upgrade. If you're setting this up for the first time, start there rather than from scratch. AI Software Testing in Practice covers the full eval lifecycle — growing the labeled dataset across model upgrades, setting regression thresholds that account for judge noise, and knowing when a score drop is a real problem versus rubric drift.

FAQ

How do I know if my LLM judge is reliable?
Run it against 20–30 human-labeled examples and measure agreement. If the judge disagrees with your labels more than 20% of the time, the rubric is wrong — tighten it and re-calibrate. Agreement above 80% on your labeled set is enough to trust the judge in CI.

Should I use the same LLM to generate and judge outputs?
No. Using the same model to evaluate its own outputs creates a blind spot for that model's specific failure modes. Use a different judge model, or judge with a stronger model than the one generating outputs.

What is position bias in LLM-as-judge and how do I avoid it?
Position bias means the judge tends to prefer whichever option it sees first in a pairwise comparison. Avoid it by either using single-answer scoring (not pairwise) or running each comparison twice with the order swapped and averaging the scores.

items.title: Stamping the downloader's email on every PDF page at download time in PHP

items.summary_html:
When a contract leaks, the first question is: whose copy was it? In Warqa, a contract management platform for companies in Saudi Arabia, every PDF and image gets the downloader's email stamped on it at download time. The original file stays clean in storage. This post shows how we built it with FPDI and TCPDF, and what we learned.

The rules we set
  1. Never change the stored original. Stamp a temporary copy for each download.
  2. The stamp names a person: the email of the logged-in user, or of the external recipient for a shared link.
  3. A failed stamp must never block work. If stamping throws, report the error and send the file.
  4. Every stamped copy gets its own tracking ID, written into the file and into the activity log.
Pick the method by file type 
$extension = strtolower(pathinfo($file, PATHINFO_EXTENSION));

if ($extension === 'pdf') {
    try { return $this->processPdf($file, $watermarkText, $title); }
    catch (Exception $e) { report($e); }
} elseif (in_array($extension, ['jpg', 'jpeg', 'png'])) {
    try { return $this->processImage($file, $watermarkText); }
    catch (Exception $e) { report($e); }
}

return $file; // other types go out unchanged

PDF and images cover almost all signed contracts and scanned documents. Word files are drafts, and a watermark in an editable file can simply be deleted.

PDF: import each page, then draw on top

FPDI imports pages of an existing PDF as templates. TCPDF then draws text over them:

$pdf = new \setasign\Fpdi\Tcpdf\Fpdi();
$pageCount = $pdf->setSourceFile($file);

for ($pageNo = 1; $pageNo <= $pageCount; $pageNo++) {
    $templateId = $pdf->importPage($pageNo);
    $size = $pdf->getTemplateSize($templateId);

    $pdf->AddPage($size['orientation'], [$size['width'], $size['height']]);
    $pdf->useTemplate($templateId);

    $this->drawWatermark($pdf, $size['width'], $size['height'], $watermarkText);
}

Keep the page size of each source page. Contracts often mix A4 portrait pages with landscape annex tables.

The stamp itself is small diagonal text, repeated in a grid across the page. The text is gray at about 10% opacity, so the document stays readable when printed. A single large stamp in the middle is easy to crop out. A grid is not.

The PDF that FPDI cannot open

The free FPDI parser does not read every compression method in newer PDFs. When it fails, we rewrite the file with Ghostscript to an older PDF version, then try again. If that fails too, rule 3 applies: report the error and send the file unstamped.

Images: GD is enough

For JPEG and PNG we use PHP's GD extension: load the image, draw the same diagonal text grid, save to a new temp file. There is no need for Imagick for this job.

A tracking ID per copy

Each stamped copy gets a new ULID. We write it into the PDF metadata keywords as TID: and save it in the activity log next to the email, IP address and user agent. If a copy turns up somewhere, its ID points to one download event, even when the visible stamp was cut off.

The download flow 
File::put($tmpPath, $attachment->getContent());

$result = app(LeakProtectionService::class)->protect(
    file: $tmpPath,
    watermarkText: $share->recipient_email,
    title: pathinfo($attachment->name, PATHINFO_FILENAME),
);

File::delete($tmpPath);
$share->recordDownload();

return response()->download($result->path)->deleteFileAfterSend();

Temp files are deleted after the response is sent. Nothing stamped stays on disk.

Where the email comes from on shared links

External recipients do not have accounts. A shared link opens only after the recipient enters a one-time code sent to their email. That verified email is the text we stamp. Without the code step, the stamp would only show the email of the person who created the link.

What a watermark does not do

A watermark does not stop a leak. It deters one and helps trace one. It works together with other controls: access permissions per folder, links that expire, and a log of who viewed or downloaded each file.

What makes F# particularly interesting is that it isn't a separate runtime universe. It uses .NET too. An F# library can be consumed by C# code. Both can use much of the same underlying framework. That's convenient. You can write enterprise business logic in C#, functional transformations in F#, and maintain an application in VB.NET, all within the same general ecosystem. Although anyone who has actually maintained a multilingual solution will tell you that technically interoperable and pleasant to maintain are not necessarily synonyms. Rich graphics and animation. And better separation between the visual interface and application logic. WPF could produce interfaces that were dramatically more sophisticated than traditional WinForms applications. It also introduced concepts such as dependency properties, routed events, and elaborate binding mechanisms. Things that were pretty cool, right up until a binding silently failed and you spent the afternoon trying to understand why a button was disabled. Then came the familiar Microsoft ecosystem question: Which UI technology should you actually use? WinForms was still around. WPF was supposed to be the modern alternative. Someone at Microsoft said: "we're gonna need a bigger boat". SO they came up with Silverlight, UWP, WinUI, and eventually .NET MAUI. And here's an important distinction: XAML isn't itself a competing UI framework. It's a declarative markup language used by multiple frameworks, including WPF, WinUI, and .NET MAUI, with differences between their implementations. (And what about Xamarin? "THERE WAS NEVER A XAMARIN"). Today, WinForms and WPF remain supported on modern .NET. WinUI is Microsoft's primary recommendation for new general-purpose Windows desktop applications. Because the underlying .NET concepts were not inherently Windows-specific, even though many framework APIs and application technologies were. Meanwhile, the original .NET Framework continues to exist, with version 4.8.1 supported on Windows. And just to complete the picture, ASP.NET Core retains the word "Core" even though the main runtime dropped it. So today: .NET Framework means the original Windows-only implementation. .NET means the modern open-source, cross-platform implementation. .NET Standard describes a compatibility-oriented API specification, not a runtime. ASP.NET Core is the modern web framework, despite the runtime's naming change. .NET Core is the former name of what evolved into modern .NET. Now let's brace ourselves for .NET Copilot which is almost certainly cooking somewhere in Redmond. 7. And Then There's PowerShell Here's a part of the .NET ecosystem that doesn't always get enough attention. PowerShell. Most people think of it as a command-line shell and scripting language, particularly associated with Windows administration. Not wrong. But PowerShell is also deeply connected to .NET. Unlike traditional Unix shells, which primarily pass text between commands, PowerShell pipelines can pass structured objects. Actual objects, with properties and methods. Those objects are frequently .NET objects. Which means a PowerShell script can access parts of the .NET ecosystem directly. Want to work with filesystem APIs? Use .NET objects. Need regular expressions? They're available. Want to instantiate framework classes or call static methods? You can do that too. PowerShell is, in many ways, a .NET automation environment disguised as a shell. And naturally, it has its own version of the great .NET identity crisis. Windows PowerShell 5.1 runs on the original .NET Framework. Modern PowerShell 7 runs on modern .NET and supports Windows, Linux, and macOS. Both can exist on the same Windows machine. And they can behave differently when scripts depend on incompatible modules or framework APIs. So now we have two PowerShell families corresponding to two .NET families. At this point, the family tree needs a database. But underneath the confusing history lies something genuinely powerful: an administrator can write a script that manipulates rich runtime objects, while developers can expose functionality that PowerShell can consume without inventing an entirely separate scripting interface. Also no. A framework? Yes, but that answer is incomplete. A runtime? Yes, but still incomplete. .NET is better understood as an entire development platform. It includes runtimes, compilers, standard libraries, SDKs, development tools, and application frameworks. It supports different languages and workloads. You can build web APIs, desktop applications, cloud services, mobile applications, games, and command-line tools. The current platform is powerful. And the shift from the original Windows-centric .NET Framework to today's open-source implementation is one of Microsoft's most significant technological transformations. There is also a wonderfully ironic outcome. Microsoft spent years building an ecosystem closely associated with Windows development. Then it invested heavily in making that ecosystem work without Windows. Developers can now build a C# application on Linux, deploy it in a Linux container, run it in the cloud, and never touch a Windows desktop. Which would have sounded strange in 2002. Somehow, all those identities coexist. Not always elegantly. Not always compatibly. And certainly not under a naming scheme that anyone would describe as intuitive. But the result is impressive.
items.summary_html:
In our last installment, we explored some of C#'s more surprising behaviors.

But C# is only part of a much bigger story.

A story involving multiple programming languages, competing user interface frameworks, a rather complicated relationship with open source, and enough product renaming to keep an entire marketing department employed for decades.

Welcome to .NET.

Or .NET Framework.

Or .NET Core.

Or just .NET again.

We'll get to that.

1. In the Beginning, There Was Windows

When Microsoft launched .NET Framework in 2002, it represented an ambitious new direction for Windows development.

At its heart was the Common Language Runtime (CLR), an execution environment providing garbage collection, memory management, exception handling, and other services that developers previously had to manage themselves.

Instead of compiling directly to native machine code, supported languages generally compiled into Common Intermediate Language (CIL), which the runtime could then execute using just-in-time compilation.

That was a pretty powerful idea.

Multiple programming languages could share a runtime, a type system, and an extensive library ecosystem.

A developer could write a library in one language and consume it from another.

Naturally, Microsoft decided that one programming language wasn't enough.

2. C#, VB.NET, and F#: Three Languages Walk Into a Runtime

C# was the obvious flagship.

Modern syntax, strong typing, object-oriented programming, and enough familiarity with Java and C++ to make developers feel at home.

But Microsoft had another a constituency to consider.

Visual Basic developers.

VB.NET: It's Visual Basic, Jim, but Not as We Know It

Visual Basic had been wildly popular for Windows application development.

Its selling point was accessibility. You could drag controls onto a form, write some event handlers, and have a functioning application without spending six months studying Windows internals.

For a generation of developers, Visual Basic was how you built business applications, full stop.

So Microsoft brought Visual Basic into .NET.

Except VB.NET wasn't simply the old Visual Basic with a new runtime.

It was substantially redesigned.

The old VB6 world included COM-based components, default form instances, and a programming model that was quite different from the CLR's object-oriented architecture.

VB.NET introduced a new type system, inheritance, structured exception handling, and the other capabilities required to participate in .NET.

That was great for architectural consistency.

Less great for developers discovering that their existing VB6 applications weren't going to migrate quite as effortlessly as they'd hoped.

Today, Visual Basic still exists in modern .NET.

But Microsoft has made its direction clear: VB will remain supported and stable, without aggressively expanding into new workloads or pursuing every new language feature introduced in C#.

Which is a polite way of saying:

"You are tolerated, former incumbent."

F#: Wait, We Also Have a Functional Language?

Then there's F#.

While C# and VB.NET largely embraced object-oriented programming, F# arrived with a functional-first philosophy.

Immutability by default.

Pattern matching.

Type inference.

Functions as first-class citizens.

And a syntax that looks refreshingly different from the sea of curly braces elsewhere in the ecosystem.

What makes F# particularly interesting is that it isn't a separate runtime universe.

It uses .NET too.

An F# library can be consumed by C# code. Both can use much of the same underlying framework.

That's convenient.

You can write enterprise business logic in C#, functional transformations in F#, and maintain an application in VB.NET, all within the same general ecosystem.

Although anyone who has actually maintained a multilingual solution will tell you that technically interoperable and pleasant to maintain are not necessarily synonyms.

The fascinating part: .NET was designed to make programming languages less important than the runtime and libraries they shared.

Twenty-four years later, C# overwhelmingly dominates the ecosystem, VB remains supported, and F# continues to serve developers who appreciate its different approach.

One platform. Three officially supported languages. Three rather different philosophies.

3. Windows Forms: Just Drag the Button On Form1

Let's talk about building user interfaces.

For many developers in the early .NET era, Windows Forms was one of the platform's most appealing features.

Open Visual Studio.

Create a form.

Drag a button onto it.

Double-click the button.

Write some code.

Keep the default icon.

Congratulations. You have a Windows application.

WinForms was wonderfully pragmatic.

Its programming model was event-driven and closely tied to traditional Windows desktop controls.

For business applications, internal tools, and database frontends, it was often exactly what developers needed.

Of course, Microsoft eventually decided that Windows application development needed something more sophisticated.

Enter WPF.

4. WPF and XAML: What if Buttons Were XML?

In 2006, Microsoft introduced Windows Presentation Foundation as part of .NET Framework 3.0.

WPF brought an entirely different approach to desktop UI development.

Instead of primarily positioning controls in a visual designer and attaching event handlers, developers could describe interfaces declaratively using XAML.

Extensible Application Markup Language.

Because apparently XML hadn't yet appeared in enough places.

To be fair, XAML enabled some powerful ideas.

Data binding.

Reusable styles and templates.

Resolution-independent layouts.

Rich graphics and animation.

And better separation between the visual interface and application logic.

WPF could produce interfaces that were dramatically more sophisticated than traditional WinForms applications.

It also introduced concepts such as dependency properties, routed events, and elaborate binding mechanisms.

Things that were pretty cool, right up until a binding silently failed and you spent the afternoon trying to understand why a button was disabled.

Then came the familiar Microsoft ecosystem question:

Which UI technology should you actually use?

WinForms was still around.

WPF was supposed to be the modern alternative.

Someone at Microsoft said: "we're gonna need a bigger boat".

SO they came up with Silverlight, UWP, WinUI, and eventually .NET MAUI.

And here's an important distinction: XAML isn't itself a competing UI framework. It's a declarative markup language used by multiple frameworks, including WPF, WinUI, and .NET MAUI, with differences between their implementations.

(And what about Xamarin? "THERE WAS NEVER A XAMARIN").

Today, WinForms and WPF remain supported on modern .NET.

WinUI is Microsoft's primary recommendation for new general-purpose Windows desktop applications.

And .NET MAUI targets multiple platforms, including Windows, macOS, Android, and iOS.

Yes, a platform famous for introducing alternatives has managed to retain several of them simultaneously.

The lesson: Microsoft rarely eliminates an old development technology simply because a newer one exists. Sometimes the future arrives, and the past just moves into the spare bedroom. Except for Xamarin.

5. Plot Twist: .NET Escapes Windows

For much of its early history, Microsoft's official .NET Framework was closely associated with Windows.

But an important part of this story happened outside Microsoft.

The Mono project began developing an open-source, cross-platform implementation of .NET in the early 2000s.

It demonstrated that .NET technology could live beyond Windows, including on Linux.

This was a mic drop moment.

Because the underlying .NET concepts were not inherently Windows-specific, even though many framework APIs and application technologies were.

Years later, Microsoft began moving toward a much more open development strategy.

It open-sourced major pieces of its developer tooling and runtime ecosystem.

Then, in 2016, .NET Core 1.0 arrived.

Open source.

Cross-platform.

Designed with modern server workloads, cloud deployment, and modularity in mind.

A Microsoft development platform running naturally on Linux would once have seemed like a fairly elaborate practical joke.

Now it was part of the official strategy.

But there was a catch.

.NET Core wasn't simply a cross-platform copy of everything in .NET Framework.

It was a different implementation with different APIs and initially a smaller surface area.

Some applications could migrate relatively easily.

Others depended on Windows-specific technologies, legacy framework components, or third-party libraries that weren't available.

And some simply couldn't be moved without significant rewrites.

But the direction was clear.

.NET was no longer synonymous with Windows.

Or proprietary software.

Which brings us to the naming department.

6. The Naming Department Has Entered the Chat

Let's recap.

We started with .NET Framework.

Then Microsoft introduced .NET Core.

Meanwhile, we had .NET Standard, which wasn't another runtime at all, but an API specification designed to help libraries work across different .NET implementations.

Then, after .NET Core 3.1, Microsoft released...

.NET 5.

Not .NET Core 4.

Not .NET Framework 5.

Just .NET 5.

Why skip four?

Partly to avoid confusion with the existing .NET Framework 4.x product line.

So Microsoft solved one naming conflict by skipping a number and dropping a word.

There was probably a PowerPoint presentation involved.

Since then, modern .NET has continued with annual version releases, reaching .NET 10 in November 2025.

Meanwhile, the original .NET Framework continues to exist, with version 4.8.1 supported on Windows.

And just to complete the picture, ASP.NET Core retains the word "Core" even though the main runtime dropped it.

So today:

  • .NET Framework means the original Windows-only implementation.
  • .NET means the modern open-source, cross-platform implementation.
  • .NET Standard describes a compatibility-oriented API specification, not a runtime.
  • ASP.NET Core is the modern web framework, despite the runtime's naming change.
  • .NET Core is the former name of what evolved into modern .NET.

Now let's brace ourselves for .NET Copilot which is almost certainly cooking somewhere in Redmond.

7. And Then There's PowerShell

Here's a part of the .NET ecosystem that doesn't always get enough attention.

PowerShell.

Most people think of it as a command-line shell and scripting language, particularly associated with Windows administration.

Not wrong.

But PowerShell is also deeply connected to .NET.

Unlike traditional Unix shells, which primarily pass text between commands, PowerShell pipelines can pass structured objects.

Actual objects, with properties and methods.

Those objects are frequently .NET objects.

Which means a PowerShell script can access parts of the .NET ecosystem directly.

Want to work with filesystem APIs?

Use .NET objects.

Need regular expressions?

They're available.

Want to instantiate framework classes or call static methods?

You can do that too.

PowerShell is, in many ways, a .NET automation environment disguised as a shell.

And naturally, it has its own version of the great .NET identity crisis.

Windows PowerShell 5.1 runs on the original .NET Framework.

Modern PowerShell 7 runs on modern .NET and supports Windows, Linux, and macOS.

Both can exist on the same Windows machine.

And they can behave differently when scripts depend on incompatible modules or framework APIs.

So now we have two PowerShell families corresponding to two .NET families.

At this point, the family tree needs a database.

But underneath the confusing history lies something genuinely powerful: an administrator can write a script that manipulates rich runtime objects, while developers can expose functionality that PowerShell can consume without inventing an entirely separate scripting interface.

It's one of .NET's more underappreciated achievements.

8. So What Exactly Is .NET?

After all that, it's worth asking the obvious question.

Is .NET a programming language?

No.

An operating system?

Also no.

A framework?

Yes, but that answer is incomplete.

A runtime?

Yes, but still incomplete.

.NET is better understood as an entire development platform.

It includes runtimes, compilers, standard libraries, SDKs, development tools, and application frameworks.

It supports different languages and workloads.

You can build web APIs, desktop applications, cloud services, mobile applications, games, and command-line tools.

The current platform is powerful.

And the shift from the original Windows-centric .NET Framework to today's open-source implementation is one of Microsoft's most significant technological transformations.

There is also a wonderfully ironic outcome.

Microsoft spent years building an ecosystem closely associated with Windows development.

Then it invested heavily in making that ecosystem work without Windows.

Developers can now build a C# application on Linux, deploy it in a Linux container, run it in the cloud, and never touch a Windows desktop.

Which would have sounded strange in 2002.

Somehow, all those identities coexist.

Not always elegantly.

Not always compatibly.

And certainly not under a naming scheme that anyone would describe as intuitive.

But the result is impressive.

items.title: Who is Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive at the center of the Jensen Huang controversy
items.summary: Jensen Huang said in a note to staffers on Sunday that he had been unfaithful to his wife. Sean Rayford/Getty Images Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in a Sunday note that he had been unfaithful to his wife. A woman named Alice Huang is at the center of the resulting scrutiny. Here's what we know about Huang, who has been an executive at Megaspeed International. Jensen Huang's note to staff on Sunday, in which he acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife, came as Nvidia opened an independent investigation into reports that he may have been the target of a "foreign intelligence effort." At the center is Alice Huang, who has been an executive for Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer. The New York Times reported in late October that US intelligence officials believe Huang, who developed a close relationship with the Nvidia CEO, was passing information to Beijing. Huang's role at Megaspeed Megaspeed first came under scrutiny after the Times reported last year that US authorities were examining whether the company and its Malaysian affiliate were helping Chinese businesses gain access to Nvidia's AI chips despite US export controls. It is unclear when Huang — who shares a last name with the CEO, but has no relation to him — first met the Nvidia chief. A 2024 LinkedIn post from the AI company NetThunder, shared during the Computex Taipei trade show, showed the pair at a bar with other technology executives. In May 2025, news footage from Taiwanese media showed them leaving a Taipei restaurant alongside other executives. However, beyond those public appearances, little is known about Huang. Singapore corporate filings identify her as Huang Le. Megaspeed International was incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International, before changing its name on March 7, 2023, according to Singapore corporate filings. A day earlier, Huang, a Chinese national, was appointed as both a director and managing director of the company, alongside another Chinese national, Cang Yang, who joined as a director. She resigned from both roles on November 10, the same day Cang also stepped down. When Huang assumed the role, corporate filings show that 7Road International HK Limited transferred all shares in the Singapore entity to Huang Le Limited, a British Virgin Islands company. That November, ownership was transferred again to Swiftdata, a Singapore company incorporated on October 31, 2023. Swiftdata remains Megaspeed’s sole shareholder. The Times reported that Megaspeed was formed after 7Road, a Chinese online gaming company, split off its Singaporean subsidiary. Before her time at Megaspeed, Huang worked as an executive director at a Shanghai investment fund that had backed 7Road and was connected to state-backed companies, per the Times. In an October response to a query from The Wall Street Journal, Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs said it had not investigated Huang over her alleged ties to Chinese intelligence or her relationship with Jensen Huang. It said, however, that the Singapore Police's investigation into Megaspeed is ongoing, and declined to comment further. Nvidia CEO's ties to Huang In response to The Times' initial reporting, Nvidia characterized Jensen Huang's interactions with Huang as routine business dealings. "Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year, John Rizzo, a spokesman for Nvidia, told the Times in late October. The Nvidia CEO himself made similar comments to Bloomberg last week. "Our relationship, our interactions, have been related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual," Huang said. On Sunday, Huang told Nvidia staff that he had been unfaithful to his wife. His note did not name Alice Huang or address the reported relationship directly. "Today's news will not slow Nvidia," a company spokesperson told Business Insider in a statement on Sunday. "Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption." Read the original article on Business Insider

When Huang assumed the role, corporate filings show that 7Road International HK Limited transferred all shares in the Singapore entity to Huang Le Limited, a British Virgin Islands company.

That November, ownership was transferred again to Swiftdata, a Singapore company incorporated on October 31, 2023. Swiftdata remains Megaspeed’s sole shareholder.

The Times reported that Megaspeed was formed after 7Road, a Chinese online gaming company, split off its Singaporean subsidiary.

Before her time at Megaspeed, Huang worked as an executive director at a Shanghai investment fund that had backed 7Road and was connected to state-backed companies, per the Times.

In an October response to a query from The Wall Street Journal, Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs said it had not investigated Huang over her alleged ties to Chinese intelligence or her relationship with Jensen Huang. It said, however, that the Singapore Police's investigation into Megaspeed is ongoing, and declined to comment further.

Nvidia CEO's ties to Huang

In response to The Times' initial reporting, Nvidia characterized Jensen Huang's interactions with Huang as routine business dealings.

"Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year, John Rizzo, a spokesman for Nvidia, told the Times in late October.

The Nvidia CEO himself made similar comments to Bloomberg last week. "Our relationship, our interactions, have been related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual," Huang said.

On Sunday, Huang told Nvidia staff that he had been unfaithful to his wife. His note did not name Alice Huang or address the reported relationship directly.

"Today's news will not slow Nvidia," a company spokesperson told Business Insider in a statement on Sunday. "Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption."

items.title: NVIDIA to Investigate CEO Jensen Huang’s Relationship with a ‘Chinese Spy’
items.summary: NVIDIA , the world’s most valuable US company with a $4.5 trillion valuation, launched an independent investigation into its Chief Executive Officer and billionaire Jensen Huang after he admitted to having a relationship outside marriage with a woman allegedly accused of working for Chinese intelligence. Huang acknowledged the relationship in an email to NVIDIA employees on November 8, apologising to his wife, family and colleagues. “I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it,” he said. The admission follows a NYT report that a Chinese executive, linked to a Singapore-based data centre company, has been funnelling information into Beijing. Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang came under scrutiny for allegedly exposing sensitive company information, raising national security concerns in the US. However, Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs Spokesperson Guo Jiakun denied any espionage charges. “The report in question is based on groundless speculation and is nothing more than an attempt to smear China,” he said. Meanwhile, the company issued a statement saying a committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation. “The Board prioritises US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” it said. “While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information.” Huang has agreed to cooperate with the investigation. NVIDIA also expressed confidence in his leadership and said it would provide further updates as appropriate. Meanwhile, Republican lawmakers in the House of Representatives have called on Huang to testify before Congress about the relationship on November 18.

items.title: Here's what smart people are saying about Nvidia's investigation of CEO Jensen Huang
items.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in a memo on Sunday that he had been "unfaithful" to his wife. Joel Saget / AFP via Getty Images Nvidia's board of directors is opening an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang. The company said it's investigating whether Huang was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort." Huang said he had been "unfaithful" to his wife in a memo to Nvidia employees. On Sunday, Nvidia said its board of directors opened an independent investigation into whether Jensen Huang had been the "target of a foreign intelligence effort." Huang shared a memo with Nvidia employees earlier in the day in which he said he had been "unfaithful" to his wife. In October, The New York Times reported that US officials believed that a Chinese intelligence asset, Alice Huang, had developed a relationship with the Nvidia CEO. Alice Huang has been an executive for Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer. As Nvidia teeters on the edge of a national security scandal, some business and tech leaders have weighed in. Here's what they're saying. Bill Ackman, CEO of Pershing Square Capital Management On Sunday, Pershing Square CEO Bill Ackman suggested people should lead with empathy when it comes to Huang. "An alert: @JensenHuang is human. And he is an incredible human. Even incredible humans make mistakes," Ackman said on X. "He takes full responsibility as he should. We should all support him and his family. Onward." Chris McGuire, senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations Chris McGuire, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, said the US Department of Commerce shared blame for the national security threat. He said the department has enacted policies that make it easy for China to access Nvidia most advanced chips. "@CommerceGov leadership knew that Jensen was sleeping with a Chinese spy and that Megaspeed was a Chinese cutout, but still actively opposed any policies to tighten export controls on Nvidia chips. Why?" he wrote in an X post on Sunday. "Commerce could have blocked chip shipments to Megaspeed the moment it found out that it was run by a Chinese spy, but it did not. Commerce has also refused to enforce regulations—which ironically remain on the books—that would require exporters to apply for a license to ship large numbers of AI chips to untrusted entities in many countries, which would prevent China from using shell companies like Megaspeed to buy controlled chips," he added. McGuire said it's important that Nvidia takes national security issues more seriously, but also called on the US Department of Commerce to "tighten up export controls." Jason Calacanis, angel investor and "All-in" host Jason Calacanis, an angel investor and host on the "All-In" podcast, said on Sunday that the US is in an urgent contest to lead the global AI industry and that Huang was central to that effort. "We need to win, for the sake of democracy and humanity. We are all in this together: the left, the right and the center. There is no time for infighting," Calacanis wrote on X. "Jensen and NVIDIA's technology are a critical target, and we need to protect them both." Calacanis called on the US to rally together against China and "go faster." "Act accordingly," he wrote. Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives Dan Ives, a partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives, said on Sunday that the situation is a stain on Huang's reputation. "This is a black eye moment for Jensen and will spark multiple congressional inquiries at a minimum and will create an overhang," Ives wrote. Michael McCaul, House Rep. Texas Rep. Michael McCaul said the US should "immediately pause" shipments of advanced AI chips to China until "we can get to the bottom of this incident and ensure our national security is not being undermined." "This is a classic move from the CCP's playbook — and another example of why it can never be trusted," he wrote. Shaun Maguire, partner at Sequoia Capital Sequoia Capital partner Shaun Maguire shared a few thoughts in an X post on Sunday. Maguire called Huang "one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation," who also did something "incredibly dumb." He called the decision "bad for America" but doubted Huang had bad intentions. "two mistakes don't make a right, and I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America's AI leadership," Maguire said. Ross Gerber, president and CEO of Gerber Kawasaki Wealth and Investment Management Ross Gerber also discussed the news in an X post on Sunday. Gerber is the president and CEO of Gerber Kawasaki Wealth & Investment Management. "Extremely disappointing to see the news regarding Jensen. A huge error of judgment and at a totally critical time for AI development. Not sure how this shakes out," he wrote. Jason Calacanis, co-host of the 'All-In' podcast Jason Calacanis said that the ban was "smart" because of the risk of terrorism. Bloomberg/Getty Images Calacanis, a startup investor and co-host of the All-In podcast, urged an end to the infighting in the US about the security concerns. "America is in a war with China and AI is the battlefield," Calacanis wrote on X on Sunday. "We need to win, for the sake of democracy and humanity." He said there was "no time for infighting" and called Huang and Nvidia's technology "a critical target" that needed protection. Calacanis said the US must "win the race for super intelligence," describing the moment as "defcon 1." Marc Lehman, independent trader Lehman, an independent trader who posts market commentary on X, said the allegations could create an overhang for Nvidia's stock. Lehman called the matter "a black eye moment for Jensen" that could prompt congressional inquiries. He said investors would focus on whether Huang would remain Nvidia's CEO. Still, Lehman said Huang's position could depend on a board investigation, which poses a risk because he is so central to Nvidia's global strategy. He added that the episode would increase scrutiny of Nvidia's chip sales to China, "which remains a key battleground issue in DC." Stephanie Ruhle, MS NOW host and business analyst Stephanie Ruhle said that AI stocks have already been unstable. Charles Sykes/Bravo via Getty Images Stephanie Ruhle, the host of MSNBC's "Money, Power, Politics" and the network's senior business analyst, said the allegations could destabilize the broader AI industry. "AI stocks were already performing a high wire act," Ruhle wrote on X. She said the Nvidia situation "could be hugely problematic for the industry," from hyperscalers to CoreWeave. Nvidia is "the tie that binds them all together and holds the ecosystem up," Ruhle wrote. She added that Huang's "clout & conviction are uniquely powerful."
