items.title: AI-assisted learning platform helps robots reason beyond literal commands
items.summary: Humans are intuitive by nature. We can sense meaning beyond the literal words that we encounter. Now, a new artificial intelligence-assisted learning platform developed by MIT engineers is enabling robots to read larger meaning into a human’s natural language commands. In a study to be presented at the annual Conference on Robot Learning this month, researchers from MIT and New York University introduce FLEX , a flexible feature-editing pipeline for robot motion-planning. With FLEX, humans can interact with a robot by giving it instructions in natural, conversational language. The robot can not only follow the instructions literally but also read into the words to draw larger generalizations that help to improve its motion-planning task. The team demonstrated FLEX in several simulated scenarios, including one in which a robot serves a cup of coffee. In these virtual scenarios, a person interacts with a robotic arm by typing commands in natural language. As the robot moves the coffee cup over a cluttered table, the person might type “Don’t spill on the laptop!” In response, the robot will reason about why it should avoid the laptop. For this, FLEX incorporates a large language model (LLM) — a type of AI system that is trained on enormous libraries of text, including social media posts, video transcriptions, and web content, which the LLM uses to identify larger trends, patterns, and generalizations. “LLMs have seen so many texts from the internet,” says study author Nathan Dennler, a postdoc in MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL). “People might have written about, ‘Oh, my phone dropped in the water and now it doesn’t work,’ or ‘I spilled coffee on my computer and now it doesn’t work.’ So LLMs pick up on the idea that liquids plus devices leads to things not working.” Through the LLM, the robot reasons that it should also avoid bumping into all electronics. In its updated path, the robot adjusts to avoid both the laptop and a nearby phone, without the person having to explicitly spell this out. “The idea is that there is some higher-level intention behind the words that you say,” Dennler says. “People naturally get this. But you have to carefully explain that to a robot, which takes time and effort. FLEX gives you an interface of communication with a robot to say, ‘When people say this, they mean that.’” The study was led by Andreea Bobu, assistant professor of aeronautics and astronautics at MIT. Co-authors are Audrey Lee SM ’26 and Ilia Sucholutsky of New York University. Beyond what we say At MIT, Bobu heads up the Collaborative Learning and Autonomy Research (CLEAR) Lab, where her group develops autonomous agents that learn to work for, with, and around people. She is focused on developing assistive and household robots that can carry out physical tasks, and reason and adapt in real-time, in response to a person’s natural, conversational commands. “Robots use math to do their trajectory planning. But we can’t expect a consumer to learn to do this math in order to tell a robot what to do,” says Dennler, who is a member of the CLEAR Lab. “Instead of having to get people to learn how to use a robot in a specific way, the goal is to interact with the robot through natural language.” There is a large effort in the robotics community to incorporate natural language into robotic learning pipelines. Various strategies include using language to clarify a task’s goal, redirect a robot’s trajectory, and update its understanding of what is a safe path to take. These existing methods use natural language to tell the robot how to physically perform a task. But a robot could potentially learn much more from what we tell it. Bobu and her colleagues are expanding what robots can learn from natural language commands. In their new study, they focused on enabling a robot to interpret a person’s underlying, unspecified preference from limited natural language commands. items.summary_html:
Humans are intuitive by nature. We can sense meaning beyond the literal words that we encounter. Now, a new artificial intelligence-assisted learning platform developed by MIT engineers is enabling robots to read larger meaning into a human’s natural language commands. 

In a study to be presented at the annual Conference on Robot Learning this month, researchers from MIT and New York University introduce FLEX, a flexible feature-editing pipeline for robot motion-planning. 

With FLEX, humans can interact with a robot by giving it instructions in natural, conversational language. The robot can not only follow the instructions literally but also read into the words to draw larger generalizations that help to improve its motion-planning task. 

The team demonstrated FLEX in several simulated scenarios, including one in which a robot serves a cup of coffee. In these virtual scenarios, a person interacts with a robotic arm by typing commands in natural language. As the robot moves the coffee cup over a cluttered table, the person might type “Don’t spill on the laptop!” In response, the robot will reason about why it should avoid the laptop. For this, FLEX incorporates a large language model (LLM) — a type of AI system that is trained on enormous libraries of text, including social media posts, video transcriptions, and web content, which the LLM uses to identify larger trends, patterns, and generalizations. 

“LLMs have seen so many texts from the internet,” says study author Nathan Dennler, a postdoc in MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL). “People might have written about, ‘Oh, my phone dropped in the water and now it doesn’t work,’ or ‘I spilled coffee on my computer and now it doesn’t work.’ So LLMs pick up on the idea that liquids plus devices leads to things not working.”

Through the LLM, the robot reasons that it should also avoid bumping into all electronics. In its updated path, the robot adjusts to avoid both the laptop and a nearby phone, without the person having to explicitly spell this out.

“The idea is that there is some higher-level intention behind the words that you say,” Dennler says. “People naturally get this. But you have to carefully explain that to a robot, which takes time and effort. FLEX gives you an interface of communication with a robot to say, ‘When people say this, they mean that.’”

The study was led by Andreea Bobu, assistant professor of aeronautics and astronautics at MIT. Co-authors are Audrey Lee SM ’26 and Ilia Sucholutsky of New York University.

Beyond what we say

At MIT, Bobu heads up the Collaborative Learning and Autonomy Research (CLEAR) Lab, where her group develops autonomous agents that learn to work for, with, and around people. She is focused on developing assistive and household robots that can carry out physical tasks, and reason and adapt in real-time, in response to a person’s natural, conversational commands. 

“Robots use math to do their trajectory planning. But we can’t expect a consumer to learn to do this math in order to tell a robot what to do,” says Dennler, who is a member of the CLEAR Lab. “Instead of having to get people to learn how to use a robot in a specific way, the goal is to interact with the robot through natural language.”

There is a large effort in the robotics community to incorporate natural language into robotic learning pipelines. Various strategies include using language to clarify a task’s goal, redirect a robot’s trajectory, and update its understanding of what is a safe path to take. These existing methods use natural language to tell the robot how to physically perform a task. But a robot could potentially learn much more from what we tell it. 

Bobu and her colleagues are expanding what robots can learn from natural language commands. In their new study, they focused on enabling a robot to interpret a person’s underlying, unspecified preference from limited natural language commands.  

Absorbing common sense

The team’s new robot learning platform, FLEX, is a three-step process that helps a robot read more into a natural language command, beyond what it is explicitly told to do. 

The first step, “Add,” instructs a robot to add a feature to its list of things in its environment that matter for the task at hand, based on a user’s natural language command. For instance, as a robot is moving a bowling ball from one location to another, a person might interject with “Don’t drop it on my mug!” The robot would then add the mug to a list of things to avoid in its path. This first step is how previous methods have worked. Every time a person makes a correction, the robot adds to its features list, and updates its trajectory to avoid those features. 

“The problem happens when your feature list becomes super long, and some features are no longer relevant because your environment may have changed,” says Dennler, who notes that this approach can grow tiresome if a person has to specify every specific feature to avoid. 

The second step, “Generalize,” is the new solution that FLEX provides. This step incorporates an LLM — in this case, GPT-4o — that considers the mug, along with any other features that the person has so far specified to avoid. The LLM automatically searches through its vast cache of data for patterns and connections among these features, to ultimately make a generalization that it should avoid objects that are fragile, even when the person has not explicitly said so. 

“LLMs have seen so many texts from the internet, from all sorts of people and places,” Dennler says. “Because they’ve trained so much on those things, some of that common sense gets absorbed into the LLM.”

In the third step, “Mask,” the robot’s standard computer vision system assesses its environment to determine what objects are no longer present, and then deletes those objects from its features list. This entire three-step process takes about five seconds. 

The team tested FLEX in simulations of a robot arm carrying out three different tasks: serving a cup of coffee, moving a candle, and carrying a bowling ball. In all three scenarios, volunteers interacted with the virtual robot by typing natural language commands, such as “Don’t spill on my laptop,” “Stay away from the stack of paper,” and “Don’t drop on the mug.” With FLEX, the robot followed all three commands literally and also reasoned at a higher level to not spill on electronics, stay away from flammable objects, and not drop its cargo on fragile things. 

“Everyone’s homes are different, and everyone cares about different things, so no robot comes out of the box knowing what matters to you,” Bobu says. “What excites me about FLEX is that it can pick that up from a sentence or two instead of asking you to spell out every rule — and that’s the difference between a robot people put up with and one they actually want in their home.” 

This work was partly supported by the MIT Generative AI Impact Consortium and the MIT Schwarzman College of Computing’s Social and Ethical Responsibilities of Computing program.

(77KB) I just asked Claude (Opus 5.5 Medium running in regular Claude Chat) to port that to Vanilla JS, in the same thread where it had built it, and got this: https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/Hidden-Reef-Egg... (98KB) They aren't identical - you can see what Claude said about that in the transcript (I don't fully understand why it differed): https://claude.ai/share/e56d163e-2793-4677-aa11-191d5058b414 But yeah, it turns out Claude Opus 5.5 is perfectly capable of 3D modeling in Vanilla JS + WebGL without Three.js. items.title: Hide your slop PR descriptions behind <details><summary>
items.summary: Most of the changes I make to my projects these days come in the form of PRs opened for me by Claude Code or Codex. The PR is my unit of work - I use them to bundle commits together, iterating on them until a feature is complete, document decisions and then merge the finished result. Today's coding agents are great at writing PR descriptions. They're too good at describing the work The problem is that they are too good. An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive. It describes the problem, the detailed solution, and the steps taken to verify it. That's a lot of information to absorb. It's not necessarily slop, but it reads like slop! It's very easy to spot an AI-written PR, and as with other forms of AI writing my instant reaction is best summarized as "I'm not reading all of that". It doesn't matter how accurate or useful the information is, I'm instantly put off by the thought that it will take me longer to read than it took the driving author to write... even when that driving author is me! I want human editorial judgement. I want someone to have thought just long enough about the PR to give me a human-approved introduction that helps me understand, at a high level, what the PR is for and whether it deserves more of my attention. I think I've found a low-effort way to do this that feels right. Hide most of it in a details/summary The HTML elements render as a collapsed heading (the summary) that can be expanded to view the larger piece of text. The code looks like this: < details > < summary > Claude Opus 5.5 summary > < h2 > The hook h2 > Plugins implement < code > register_agent_reference_types(datasette) code > ... details > When rendered, it looks like this : Crucially, is supported in GitHub Markdown . You can drop those tags directly into an issue comment or PR description and GitHub will hide the details and display just the summary plus an expansion arrow. I've started using this for my AI-generated pull requests. The opening paragraph of my PRs will be carefully selected to act as a high-level explanation of what's going on - the shortest text a human can read that will help get them up to speed. I'll sometimes throw in a screenshot as well, since images are often the best way to quickly illustrate a new feature. The full agent-written essay then follows in a . I use the model name and often the effort level as that summary, to make it abundantly clear what is going on - "Claude Opus 5.5 Medium" for example. My PRs don't feel nearly as sloppy now! The information is all still there, but a reader can glance at it and get the top, human-curated information without their eyes glazing over at multiple paragraphs of agent-written details. I don't always write the introduction myself - sometimes the agent has given me what I need already, hidden away in the avalanche of other text. My promise to the reader is that the short opener will represent my human judgement as to what is definitely worth their time. Here are some recent examples where I've used this pattern, including the opener I used: datasette PR #3052: Redesign row page as a vertical list of fields - "The row page showed its single row as a one-row table. For wide tables, like a 46-column GitHub repos table, that scrolled far off to the right and left most of the page blank." (then a screenshot) datasette PR #3043: Pagination bar showing which rows are on the current page - "Table pages that span more than one page now make it obvious where you are, and offer navigation at the top of the page as well as the bottom." (plus screenshot) datasette PR #3042: Load edit-tools.js on demand via a small loader - " edit-tools.js (~220KB) was loaded on every table, row and database page, even for users who couldn't edit anything. Now only load it for users who can edit when they first interact with an edit feature (including mouse over an edit link)." datasette-agent PR #51: register_agent_reference_types plugin hook - "Lets plugins add their own kinds of item to the # tagging in the chat composer using a new register_agent_reference_types(datasette) plugin hook." - pictured above. llm PR #1838: Add llm openai endpoint add/list/remove/path commands - "Adds commands for managing the records in extra-openai-models.yaml , so OpenAI-compatible endpoints can be saved from the command line instead of by hand-editing YAML." - then copied --help output. The mnemonic I used to have trouble remembering the order of the tags - is it or ? Here are two tricks that helped me. First, and most obviously, the is clearly the bit where you summarize the details. That's the tag for your line of text that can be clicked to expand - the element must then wrap everything else. An even better trick is to always refer to these two tags as "details-summary". "details-summary" is two syllables followed by three syllables. That rolls off the tongue more smoothly than the three-two punch of "summary-details". Say "details-summary" out loud just a few times and you'll never forget the order of the tags again. (I still wish GitHub would add a button to their Markdown editor for this - partly to save me painstakingly typing it on my mobile keyboard, and partly to help spread the word to more GitHub users that this feature exists.) Tags: github , html , markdown , ai , datasette , generative-ai , llms , ai-assisted-programming , llm , coding-agents

They're too good at describing the work

The problem is that they are too good. An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive. It describes the problem, the detailed solution, and the steps taken to verify it. That's a lot of information to absorb.

It's not necessarily slop, but it reads like slop!

It's very easy to spot an AI-written PR, and as with other forms of AI writing my instant reaction is best summarized as "I'm not reading all of that". It doesn't matter how accurate or useful the information is, I'm instantly put off by the thought that it will take me longer to read than it took the driving author to write... even when that driving author is me!

I want human editorial judgement. I want someone to have thought just long enough about the PR to give me a human-approved introduction that helps me understand, at a high level, what the PR is for and whether it deserves more of my attention.

I think I've found a low-effort way to do this that feels right.

Hide most of it in a details/summary

The HTML elements render as a collapsed heading (the summary) that can be expanded to view the larger piece of text. The code looks like this:

<details>
  <summary>Claude Opus 5.5summary>
  <h2>The hookh2>
  Plugins implement <code>register_agent_reference_types(datasette)code>...
details>

When rendered, it looks like this:

Crucially, is supported in GitHub Markdown. You can drop those tags directly into an issue comment or PR description and GitHub will hide the details and display just the summary plus an expansion arrow.

I've started using this for my AI-generated pull requests.

The opening paragraph of my PRs will be carefully selected to act as a high-level explanation of what's going on - the shortest text a human can read that will help get them up to speed.

I'll sometimes throw in a screenshot as well, since images are often the best way to quickly illustrate a new feature.

The full agent-written essay then follows in a . I use the model name and often the effort level as that summary, to make it abundantly clear what is going on - "Claude Opus 5.5 Medium" for example.

My PRs don't feel nearly as sloppy now! The information is all still there, but a reader can glance at it and get the top, human-curated information without their eyes glazing over at multiple paragraphs of agent-written details.

I don't always write the introduction myself - sometimes the agent has given me what I need already, hidden away in the avalanche of other text. My promise to the reader is that the short opener will represent my human judgement as to what is definitely worth their time.

Here are some recent examples where I've used this pattern, including the opener I used:

  • datasette PR #3052: Redesign row page as a vertical list of fields - "The row page showed its single row as a one-row table. For wide tables, like a 46-column GitHub repos table, that scrolled far off to the right and left most of the page blank." (then a screenshot)
  • datasette PR #3043: Pagination bar showing which rows are on the current page - "Table pages that span more than one page now make it obvious where you are, and offer navigation at the top of the page as well as the bottom." (plus screenshot)
  • datasette PR #3042: Load edit-tools.js on demand via a small loader - "edit-tools.js (~220KB) was loaded on every table, row and database page, even for users who couldn't edit anything. Now only load it for users who can edit when they first interact with an edit feature (including mouse over an edit link)."
  • datasette-agent PR #51: register_agent_reference_types plugin hook - "Lets plugins add their own kinds of item to the # tagging in the chat composer using a new register_agent_reference_types(datasette) plugin hook." - pictured above.
  • llm PR #1838: Add llm openai endpoint add/list/remove/path commands - "Adds commands for managing the records in extra-openai-models.yaml, so OpenAI-compatible endpoints can be saved from the command line instead of by hand-editing YAML." - then copied --help output.
The mnemonic

I used to have trouble remembering the order of the tags - is it or ?

Here are two tricks that helped me.

First, and most obviously, the is clearly the bit where you summarize the details. That's the tag for your line of text that can be clicked to expand - the element must then wrap everything else.

An even better trick is to always refer to these two tags as "details-summary".

"details-summary" is two syllables followed by three syllables. That rolls off the tongue more smoothly than the three-two punch of "summary-details".

Say "details-summary" out loud just a few times and you'll never forget the order of the tags again.

(I still wish GitHub would add a button to their Markdown editor for this - partly to save me painstakingly typing it on my mobile keyboard, and partly to help spread the word to more GitHub users that this feature exists.)

items.title: Hexaware to Drive EBRD’s Banking Tech Ops for 5 Years
items.summary: The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), a multilateral development bank operating across 40 economies, has selected Hexaware Technologies under a five-year framework to develop the bank's technology operations. The agreement covers the EBRD's Run-Change-Transform technology portfolio and aims to support its technology blueprint, Northstar. The scope includes software engineering, IT operations, cybersecurity, cloud, data analytics, SAP application support, and treasury risk operations. Hexaware said it would help integrate AI into the bank's operations, automate processes, and identify opportunities to improve delivery efficiency. The financial details of the deal were not disclosed. Under the framework, Hexaware will work as part of the EBRD's technology organisation, with onshore and offshore centres supporting delivery. Hexaware plans to deploy three of its platforms: RapidX for agentic software development, Amaze for data engineering and modernisation, and Tensai Reasoning Ops for intelligent operations and AIOps. The arrangement builds on an existing relationship between the two organisations. "We want our strategic partners operating as part of one team, no matter where they are based geographically," Simon Reeves, Director of Technology at the EBRD, said in a statement. The partnership's integrated delivery model also has parallels with Hexaware's forward-deployed engineering capabilities , which involve engineers working directly in client environments. Hexaware also intends to take this approach to other international financial institutions and multilateral development banks.

items.title: LTM, ServiceNow to Expand Partnership to Scale AI Agent Deployments
items.summary: IT services company LTM and US enterprise software company ServiceNow have announced plans to expand their partnership and develop joint AI agent offerings for more than 700 shared customers. LTM will use its internal deployment of 1,500 ServiceNow AI agents as a reference for these customer engagements. The partnership will combine ServiceNow’s AI Platform with LTM’s engineering and consulting capabilities. ServiceNow's Super Intelligence Control Tower provides a central system for AI inventory and risk oversight. LTM expects the deployment to improve AI asset management and efficiency by up to 80%. The company did not disclose the baseline or methodology behind this estimate. As enterprises deploy more AI agents, questions around access permissions and accountability are becoming more pressing. Kulmeet Bawa, GVP and Managing Director, ServiceNow India and SAARC, highlighted these concerns in the announcement. “But every agent is a new identity with enterprise access, and most companies can't say where their agents are, what they're doing, or who's accountable,” Bawa said. He added that the ServiceNow Super Intelligence Control Tower gave LTM visibility and control over its AI agents. The ServiceNow platform is already used across LTM’s cybersecurity, human resources, IT, and project delivery operations. The companies said the platform had helped reduce IT ticket volumes and streamline security operations. LTM also reported up to 87% faster senior management review cycles. Other IT services companies are pursuing similar arrangements with enterprise software providers. Accenture and Workday have established a forward-deployed engineering programme for AI agents , bringing engineers closer to customer deployments in HR and finance. The companies did not disclose the financial terms of the expanded partnership or provide a timeline for the joint offerings.

items.title: ASML Has More Demand Than Machines. How It Allocates Them Is the Real Story
items.summary: ASML expects its sales to jump about 36% in 2026, yet management now says the machines it plans to build in 2027 and 2028 will not cover what customers want to buy. A supplier in that position stops chasing orders. It decides who gets production slots, on what terms and at what price. A Record Year on Fewer Machines The Netherlands-based chipmaking equipment maker reported record third-quarter sales of €11.7 billion on October 14, with a gross margin of 57.5% against 51.6% a year earlier. It guides full-year 2026 sales to between €44 billion and €45 billion, up from €32.7 billion in 2025. For the fourth quarter it guides sales of €14.2 billion to €15.2 billion at a gross margin around 57%, roughly where the third quarter landed. ASML is the world’s only maker of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography systems, the machines that print the smallest circuit features on advanced chips. Those results rest on fewer machines. ASML sold 327 lithography systems in 2025, down from 418 in 2024, while net sales rose 15.6%. Service and upgrade sales, which ASML calls Installed Base Management, climbed from €6.5 billion to €8.2 billion. In the third quarter they reached €3.3 billion, 68% above a year earlier and almost €400 million above ASML’s own guidance. Unit sales have started to recover, with 121 systems in the third quarter against 91 in the second, but the service business still grows fastest. Installed Base Management made up about 23% of ASML’s sales in 2024, about 25% in 2025 and about 28% in the third quarter. Chief Financial Officer Roger Dassen guided it to grow around 50% in 2026, compared with more than 45% for EUV system sales and around 20% for non-EUV systems. A 50% rise on 2025’s €8.2 billion implies roughly €12.3 billion. Dassen credited the margin beat to very high-margin upgrade products and called upgrade demand an important swing factor for margins in 2027 and beyond. Net income of €5.0 billion also includes about €500 million from a higher valuation of ASML’s stake in French AI company Mistral AI, Dassen said. Operating income of €5.2 billion, a 44.4% margin, is the cleaner measure of what the core business earned. Supply Sets the Ceiling ASML’s third-quarter release says customers keep raising their demand forecasts. The same release says ASML’s planned supply for 2027 and 2028 “will not fully meet the demand of our customers.” Some customers have started asking to place orders for 2029 and even 2030. ASML’s 2026 capacity is around 65 low-NA EUV systems, up from 44 shipped in 2025, and around 130 deep ultraviolet (DUV) immersion systems, the workhorses that print most layers on a chip. The company plans to add 30% to both in 2027 and is now studying more than the further 30% it had been considering for 2028. Thirty percent on a base of 65 works out to roughly 85 EUV machines, though management declined to give 2027 or 2028 unit figures, calling it far too early. In July, Dassen said ASML was already close to being fully covered with orders for low-NA EUV in 2027. Faster tools offer a second way to add supply. ASML’s release says it continues to provide “significant wafer capacity” to customers through its productivity upgrade portfolio, and Dassen called the ability to raise capacity through upgrades on the same footprint “very compelling for our customers.” A fab that cannot get another scanner can still push more wafers through the ones it has. That option helps explain why upgrades lead ASML’s 2026 growth guidance. The constraint sits with suppliers. Chief Executive Officer Christophe Fouquet said the main challenge is getting suppliers to grow about 30% a year, noting that EUV output rose roughly 50% this year. Dassen added that some suppliers need help to get there. ASML works with about 5,100 suppliers and sources roughly 80% of its bill of materials externally, its annual report says. Fouquet does not see Zeiss as a bottleneck for the expansion under discussion. Carl Zeiss SMT of Germany is ASML’s sole supplier of lenses, mirrors and other critical optical components, and ASML holds a 24.9% stake in the business. The annual report treats the relationship as a risk factor. It says Zeiss’s production capacity limits how many systems ASML can build, and it states the worst case plainly: if Zeiss ended supply or could not produce optics for a prolonged period, ASML would “effectively cease to be able to conduct our business.” Both statements can hold: the filing describes a structural dependency, and the call describes where the pinch sits today. Capacity also depends on ASML’s own factories. In September the company broke ground on a second industrial campus at the Brainport Industries Campus North in Eindhoven, the Netherlands, which it says will add manufacturing capacity for its planned growth. The first phase, expected to be completed in 2029, will house at least 3,000 employees, which puts it after the 2027 and 2028 supply window. ASML describes the “flow factory” planned there as a new operating model for its TWINSCAN production, designed to make module production and installation faster. Memory Has Joined Logic in the Queue The customers lining up for slots are changing. Dassen guided 2026 memory system sales to grow around 75% and logic system sales around 10%, with advanced logic up more than 25%. In the third quarter, system sales split 54% logic and 46% memory. Memory makers now account for nearly as much of ASML’s system sales as logic chipmakers do. Customer filings show the same pressure. SK hynix of South Korea disclosed on March 24, in a regulatory filing, a purchase of 11.9 trillion won (about $7.9 billion) of EUV lithography equipment from ASML, valid through 2027, and analysts estimate it covers roughly 30 machines. TSMC of Taiwan, the world’s largest contract chipmaker, kept its 2026 capital spending guidance at $60 billion to $64 billion on October 15. Its chief financial officer, Wendell Huang, said spending from 2026 to 2028 would exceed the previous three years and keep rising with customer demand. Orders and budgets of that size show the volume ASML must weigh before it accepts anything for 2029 and 2030. Down Payments and Price Rises Do the Rationing Dassen told analysts that an ASML order carries two commitments. The first is a down payment that is “enough to hurt.” The second is a purchase order that costs more than the deposit to unwind, which is why customers do not sign one lightly. ASML has not accepted any of the 2029 and 2030 orders customers have offered. Dassen said the company wants to total all requests and compare them with future capacity first, so it does not fill slots for some customers and then tell another it is sold out. Fouquet said ASML checks the demand against customers’ fab construction plans and treats it as real rather than inflated by customers trying to secure a place in line. Price is the second lever. ASML has raised prices on what Dassen calls its most critical products, the high-volume manufacturing machines that deliver the most value to customers. The increases do not affect 2026, start to show in 2027 and take full effect from 2028, and upgrade prices follow tool prices. Dassen and Fouquet both said ASML does not plan to repeat the increase every year. ASML says it wants prices tied to the value of its tools so that it never has to negotiate cuts if the market softens. The implication is that ASML is locking in planning certainty through contracts that outlast the shortage, while customers that commit secure their place in the queue. Cash arrives before delivery, slots go out on ASML’s schedule and the price base rises from 2028. Fouquet called the customer discussions more than constructive. Customers funding ASML ahead of delivery is not new. In 2012, Intel, TSMC and Samsung agreed to buy an aggregate 23% of ASML for €3.85 billion in cash and to commit €1.38 billion to research and development, a programme ASML said would accelerate the development of EUV lithography. Samsung’s piece alone was a 3% stake for €503 million plus €276 million for research over five years. The history helps explain the current arrangement: customers helped pay to make EUV exist, and they now commit cash to secure its output. The Balance Sheet Replaces the Order Book ASML’s last reported bookings came with its fourth-quarter 2025 results: €13.2 billion of net bookings and a backlog of €38.8 billion at year-end. The 2026 results releases carry no bookings figure. Analysts now look elsewhere for a gauge of demand. The substitute is cash. Free cash flow swung from an outflow of €2.6 billion in the first quarter to an inflow of €11.4 billion in the third, which Dassen tied to customer order momentum and the related down payments. The fourth quarter of 2025, the one that produced those €13.2 billion of bookings, brought €10.9 billion of free cash flow. Non-current liabilities rose from €6.2 billion to €12.0 billion in one quarter. Dassen confirmed that the line includes down payments and called it a lagging but useful proxy for order intake. Cash received before delivery is not revenue, and it does not repeat by itself. Third-quarter free cash flow was more than double that quarter’s operating income, and ASML did not put a figure on the prepayment share during the call. Cash and short-term investments rose from €7.6 billion to €12.7 billion over the quarter even after ASML repurchased about €4.1 billion of its shares, and some of that balance is customer prepayments. The deposit line now carries information that bookings used to carry, and it arrives with a delay. High-NA Shows Where Customers Set the Pace Rationing works for products customers cannot buy anywhere else, and low-NA EUV is one of them. ASML’s newer High-NA platform sits in a different position. The company sold one High-NA system in the third quarter, and adoption follows each customer’s own schedule. On July 15, ASML said Intel Foundry had entered high-volume manufacturing on a subset of its Core Ultra Series 3 processors, built on Intel’s 18A process with High-NA, and called it the first high-volume logic product made with the technology. The product ships at yields matched to ASML’s low-NA NXE platform, ASML said, and specific 18A layers are now dual-qualified on High-NA. Fouquet noted that Intel has announced it exposed more than 1 million wafers. Other customers sit further out. Fouquet said Samsung and TSMC plan to bring High-NA into high-volume manufacturing in 2028 and 2030. ASML and TSMC also announced in September a push to move the industry from 6-inch to 12-inch photomasks, with a pilot line by 2031 and system readiness for advanced-node production by 2033, while High-NA enters production first on the 6-inch masks. The shortage ASML manages today applies to the tools customers already run at scale, low-NA EUV and DUV immersion. China Falls to a Fifth of Sales, and the Rules Are Still Moving China accounted for 36.1% of ASML’s total net sales in 2024 and 29.1% in 2025. ASML guides China to around 20% of total net sales for 2026. Twenty percent of the €44.5 billion midpoint is roughly €8.9 billion, slightly under the €9.5 billion of 2025, so the share falls mostly because the rest of the business is growing. ASML’s annual report says Dutch, US and other laws require export licences for EUV systems and specific DUV immersion systems. A bill in the US Congress would go further. The Multilateral Alignment of Technology Controls on Hardware Act, known as the MATCH Act, would bar sales of DUV immersion systems to a list of named Chinese chipmakers, including SMIC and Huawei, and restrict servicing of machines already installed at those facilities. It would give the Netherlands and Japan 150 days to match US controls before Washington could act on its own by extending US jurisdiction to foreign-built machines that contain US technology. The bill cleared the US House Foreign Affairs Committee in April, and backers have attached it to the US Senate’s version of the annual defense authorization bill. It remains a proposal. In answers to parliamentary questions on May 12, Dutch Foreign Trade Minister Sjoerdsma wrote that the cabinet opposes the extraterritorial effect of the American proposal, which he said could require licences for maintaining equipment at certain end users. He added that the effect on semiconductor companies’ revenue, Dutch firms included, could be significant but depends on the implementing rules and any exceptions. ASML’s China guidance covers total net sales, which combine new machines and servicing, so a servicing ban would reach the installed base as well as future machine sales. Fouquet argues that the risk of serious Chinese competition stays low as long as ASML keeps market access on reasonable terms, and he added that Chinese chipmakers denied access to some tools would have far more reason to build their own. On the October call he put the likelihood of major competition in China as “still pretty low.” Reuters reported in December 2025, citing unnamed sources, that a team in Shenzhen has built a prototype that generates EUV light but does not yet make chips, with a target of producing chips in 2028, though other experts consider 2030 more likely. What Has to Hold One customer accounted for €7.8 billion, or 23.9%, of ASML’s 2025 net sales, up from 16.6% in 2024. The annual report warns that losing a major customer, or a sharp cut or delay in its orders, could materially hurt results. It also says customers have scaled back capacity additions before, and that after years of hiring, ASML would struggle to cut costs quickly in a downturn. The last deep downturn shows what a reversal costs. In 2009, ASML’s net sales fell 46.0% to €1,596 million from €2,954 million, shipments dropped to 70 systems from 151, and the company reported a net loss of €151 million. ASML has more cushion now: services make up about a quarter of revenue and the year-end 2025 backlog stood at €38.8 billion. It also no longer reports quarterly bookings, so investors would see an order slowdown less directly. Every demand signal in the third-quarter release traces back to one assumption: how big and how long-lasting customers expect AI investment to be. The down payments make cancellation expensive, which is their purpose. They do not change the fact that the forecasts depend on how long AI spending lasts. Datafloq Teamdatafloq-editorialEdit Profile ASML’s own long-range plan shows how fast the ground has moved. Guidance for 2026 already matches the low end of the 2030 scenarios the company set out in November 2024: revenue of €44 billion to €60 billion at a gross margin of 56% to 60%. ASML calls those figures an opportunity and says it will update its longer-term views at a Capital Markets Day on June 10, 2027. Dassen said ASML will give its gross margin outlook for 2027 with its fourth-quarter results in January. Until then, the evidence sits in places ASML does not headline: the deposit line on its balance sheet, the growth rate of its suppliers and the terms of the 2029 and 2030 orders it has not yet accepted. ASML has shown it can turn scarcity into prepayments and higher prices, and holding both depends on suppliers that must keep growing about 30% a year and on customers whose AI budgets it does not control.
items.summary_html:
ASML expects its sales to jump about 36% in 2026, yet management now says the machines it plans to build in 2027 and 2028 will not cover what customers want to buy. A supplier in that position stops chasing orders. It decides who gets production slots, on what terms and at what price.

A Record Year on Fewer Machines

The Netherlands-based chipmaking equipment maker reported record third-quarter sales of €11.7 billion on October 14, with a gross margin of 57.5% against 51.6% a year earlier. It guides full-year 2026 sales to between €44 billion and €45 billion, up from €32.7 billion in 2025. For the fourth quarter it guides sales of €14.2 billion to €15.2 billion at a gross margin around 57%, roughly where the third quarter landed. ASML is the world’s only maker of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography systems, the machines that print the smallest circuit features on advanced chips.

Those results rest on fewer machines. ASML sold 327 lithography systems in 2025, down from 418 in 2024, while net sales rose 15.6%. Service and upgrade sales, which ASML calls Installed Base Management, climbed from €6.5 billion to €8.2 billion. In the third quarter they reached €3.3 billion, 68% above a year earlier and almost €400 million above ASML’s own guidance.

Unit sales have started to recover, with 121 systems in the third quarter against 91 in the second, but the service business still grows fastest. Installed Base Management made up about 23% of ASML’s sales in 2024, about 25% in 2025 and about 28% in the third quarter. Chief Financial Officer Roger Dassen guided it to grow around 50% in 2026, compared with more than 45% for EUV system sales and around 20% for non-EUV systems. A 50% rise on 2025’s €8.2 billion implies roughly €12.3 billion.

Dassen credited the margin beat to very high-margin upgrade products and called upgrade demand an important swing factor for margins in 2027 and beyond. Net income of €5.0 billion also includes about €500 million from a higher valuation of ASML’s stake in French AI company Mistral AI, Dassen said. Operating income of €5.2 billion, a 44.4% margin, is the cleaner measure of what the core business earned.

Supply Sets the Ceiling

ASML’s third-quarter release says customers keep raising their demand forecasts. The same release says ASML’s planned supply for 2027 and 2028 “will not fully meet the demand of our customers.” Some customers have started asking to place orders for 2029 and even 2030.

ASML’s 2026 capacity is around 65 low-NA EUV systems, up from 44 shipped in 2025, and around 130 deep ultraviolet (DUV) immersion systems, the workhorses that print most layers on a chip. The company plans to add 30% to both in 2027 and is now studying more than the further 30% it had been considering for 2028. Thirty percent on a base of 65 works out to roughly 85 EUV machines, though management declined to give 2027 or 2028 unit figures, calling it far too early. In July, Dassen said ASML was already close to being fully covered with orders for low-NA EUV in 2027.

Faster tools offer a second way to add supply. ASML’s release says it continues to provide “significant wafer capacity” to customers through its productivity upgrade portfolio, and Dassen called the ability to raise capacity through upgrades on the same footprint “very compelling for our customers.” A fab that cannot get another scanner can still push more wafers through the ones it has. That option helps explain why upgrades lead ASML’s 2026 growth guidance.

The constraint sits with suppliers. Chief Executive Officer Christophe Fouquet said the main challenge is getting suppliers to grow about 30% a year, noting that EUV output rose roughly 50% this year. Dassen added that some suppliers need help to get there. ASML works with about 5,100 suppliers and sources roughly 80% of its bill of materials externally, its annual report says.

Fouquet does not see Zeiss as a bottleneck for the expansion under discussion. Carl Zeiss SMT of Germany is ASML’s sole supplier of lenses, mirrors and other critical optical components, and ASML holds a 24.9% stake in the business. The annual report treats the relationship as a risk factor. It says Zeiss’s production capacity limits how many systems ASML can build, and it states the worst case plainly: if Zeiss ended supply or could not produce optics for a prolonged period, ASML would “effectively cease to be able to conduct our business.” Both statements can hold: the filing describes a structural dependency, and the call describes where the pinch sits today.

Capacity also depends on ASML’s own factories. In September the company broke ground on a second industrial campus at the Brainport Industries Campus North in Eindhoven, the Netherlands, which it says will add manufacturing capacity for its planned growth. The first phase, expected to be completed in 2029, will house at least 3,000 employees, which puts it after the 2027 and 2028 supply window. ASML describes the “flow factory” planned there as a new operating model for its TWINSCAN production, designed to make module production and installation faster.

Memory Has Joined Logic in the Queue

The customers lining up for slots are changing. Dassen guided 2026 memory system sales to grow around 75% and logic system sales around 10%, with advanced logic up more than 25%. In the third quarter, system sales split 54% logic and 46% memory. Memory makers now account for nearly as much of ASML’s system sales as logic chipmakers do.

Customer filings show the same pressure. SK hynix of South Korea disclosed on March 24, in a regulatory filing, a purchase of 11.9 trillion won (about $7.9 billion) of EUV lithography equipment from ASML, valid through 2027, and analysts estimate it covers roughly 30 machines. TSMC of Taiwan, the world’s largest contract chipmaker, kept its 2026 capital spending guidance at $60 billion to $64 billion on October 15. Its chief financial officer, Wendell Huang, said spending from 2026 to 2028 would exceed the previous three years and keep rising with customer demand. Orders and budgets of that size show the volume ASML must weigh before it accepts anything for 2029 and 2030.

Down Payments and Price Rises Do the Rationing

Dassen told analysts that an ASML order carries two commitments. The first is a down payment that is “enough to hurt.” The second is a purchase order that costs more than the deposit to unwind, which is why customers do not sign one lightly.

ASML has not accepted any of the 2029 and 2030 orders customers have offered. Dassen said the company wants to total all requests and compare them with future capacity first, so it does not fill slots for some customers and then tell another it is sold out. Fouquet said ASML checks the demand against customers’ fab construction plans and treats it as real rather than inflated by customers trying to secure a place in line.

Price is the second lever. ASML has raised prices on what Dassen calls its most critical products, the high-volume manufacturing machines that deliver the most value to customers. The increases do not affect 2026, start to show in 2027 and take full effect from 2028, and upgrade prices follow tool prices. Dassen and Fouquet both said ASML does not plan to repeat the increase every year. ASML says it wants prices tied to the value of its tools so that it never has to negotiate cuts if the market softens.

The implication is that ASML is locking in planning certainty through contracts that outlast the shortage, while customers that commit secure their place in the queue. Cash arrives before delivery, slots go out on ASML’s schedule and the price base rises from 2028. Fouquet called the customer discussions more than constructive.

Customers funding ASML ahead of delivery is not new. In 2012, Intel, TSMC and Samsung agreed to buy an aggregate 23% of ASML for €3.85 billion in cash and to commit €1.38 billion to research and development, a programme ASML said would accelerate the development of EUV lithography. Samsung’s piece alone was a 3% stake for €503 million plus €276 million for research over five years. The history helps explain the current arrangement: customers helped pay to make EUV exist, and they now commit cash to secure its output.

The Balance Sheet Replaces the Order Book

ASML’s last reported bookings came with its fourth-quarter 2025 results: €13.2 billion of net bookings and a backlog of €38.8 billion at year-end. The 2026 results releases carry no bookings figure. Analysts now look elsewhere for a gauge of demand.

The substitute is cash. Free cash flow swung from an outflow of €2.6 billion in the first quarter to an inflow of €11.4 billion in the third, which Dassen tied to customer order momentum and the related down payments. The fourth quarter of 2025, the one that produced those €13.2 billion of bookings, brought €10.9 billion of free cash flow. Non-current liabilities rose from €6.2 billion to €12.0 billion in one quarter. Dassen confirmed that the line includes down payments and called it a lagging but useful proxy for order intake.

Cash received before delivery is not revenue, and it does not repeat by itself. Third-quarter free cash flow was more than double that quarter’s operating income, and ASML did not put a figure on the prepayment share during the call. Cash and short-term investments rose from €7.6 billion to €12.7 billion over the quarter even after ASML repurchased about €4.1 billion of its shares, and some of that balance is customer prepayments. The deposit line now carries information that bookings used to carry, and it arrives with a delay.

High-NA Shows Where Customers Set the Pace

Rationing works for products customers cannot buy anywhere else, and low-NA EUV is one of them. ASML’s newer High-NA platform sits in a different position. The company sold one High-NA system in the third quarter, and adoption follows each customer’s own schedule.

On July 15, ASML said Intel Foundry had entered high-volume manufacturing on a subset of its Core Ultra Series 3 processors, built on Intel’s 18A process with High-NA, and called it the first high-volume logic product made with the technology. The product ships at yields matched to ASML’s low-NA NXE platform, ASML said, and specific 18A layers are now dual-qualified on High-NA. Fouquet noted that Intel has announced it exposed more than 1 million wafers.

Other customers sit further out. Fouquet said Samsung and TSMC plan to bring High-NA into high-volume manufacturing in 2028 and 2030. ASML and TSMC also announced in September a push to move the industry from 6-inch to 12-inch photomasks, with a pilot line by 2031 and system readiness for advanced-node production by 2033, while High-NA enters production first on the 6-inch masks. The shortage ASML manages today applies to the tools customers already run at scale, low-NA EUV and DUV immersion.

China Falls to a Fifth of Sales, and the Rules Are Still Moving

China accounted for 36.1% of ASML’s total net sales in 2024 and 29.1% in 2025. ASML guides China to around 20% of total net sales for 2026. Twenty percent of the €44.5 billion midpoint is roughly €8.9 billion, slightly under the €9.5 billion of 2025, so the share falls mostly because the rest of the business is growing.

ASML’s annual report says Dutch, US and other laws require export licences for EUV systems and specific DUV immersion systems. A bill in the US Congress would go further. The Multilateral Alignment of Technology Controls on Hardware Act, known as the MATCH Act, would bar sales of DUV immersion systems to a list of named Chinese chipmakers, including SMIC and Huawei, and restrict servicing of machines already installed at those facilities. It would give the Netherlands and Japan 150 days to match US controls before Washington could act on its own by extending US jurisdiction to foreign-built machines that contain US technology.

The bill cleared the US House Foreign Affairs Committee in April, and backers have attached it to the US Senate’s version of the annual defense authorization bill. It remains a proposal. In answers to parliamentary questions on May 12, Dutch Foreign Trade Minister Sjoerdsma wrote that the cabinet opposes the extraterritorial effect of the American proposal, which he said could require licences for maintaining equipment at certain end users. He added that the effect on semiconductor companies’ revenue, Dutch firms included, could be significant but depends on the implementing rules and any exceptions. ASML’s China guidance covers total net sales, which combine new machines and servicing, so a servicing ban would reach the installed base as well as future machine sales.

Fouquet argues that the risk of serious Chinese competition stays low as long as ASML keeps market access on reasonable terms, and he added that Chinese chipmakers denied access to some tools would have far more reason to build their own. On the October call he put the likelihood of major competition in China as “still pretty low.” Reuters reported in December 2025, citing unnamed sources, that a team in Shenzhen has built a prototype that generates EUV light but does not yet make chips, with a target of producing chips in 2028, though other experts consider 2030 more likely.

What Has to Hold

One customer accounted for €7.8 billion, or 23.9%, of ASML’s 2025 net sales, up from 16.6% in 2024. The annual report warns that losing a major customer, or a sharp cut or delay in its orders, could materially hurt results. It also says customers have scaled back capacity additions before, and that after years of hiring, ASML would struggle to cut costs quickly in a downturn.

The last deep downturn shows what a reversal costs. In 2009, ASML’s net sales fell 46.0% to €1,596 million from €2,954 million, shipments dropped to 70 systems from 151, and the company reported a net loss of €151 million. ASML has more cushion now: services make up about a quarter of revenue and the year-end 2025 backlog stood at €38.8 billion. It also no longer reports quarterly bookings, so investors would see an order slowdown less directly.

Every demand signal in the third-quarter release traces back to one assumption: how big and how long-lasting customers expect AI investment to be. The down payments make cancellation expensive, which is their purpose. They do not change the fact that the forecasts depend on how long AI spending lasts.

Datafloq Teamdatafloq-editorialEdit Profile

ASML’s own long-range plan shows how fast the ground has moved. Guidance for 2026 already matches the low end of the 2030 scenarios the company set out in November 2024: revenue of €44 billion to €60 billion at a gross margin of 56% to 60%. ASML calls those figures an opportunity and says it will update its longer-term views at a Capital Markets Day on June 10, 2027.

Dassen said ASML will give its gross margin outlook for 2027 with its fourth-quarter results in January. Until then, the evidence sits in places ASML does not headline: the deposit line on its balance sheet, the growth rate of its suppliers and the terms of the 2029 and 2030 orders it has not yet accepted. ASML has shown it can turn scarcity into prepayments and higher prices, and holding both depends on suppliers that must keep growing about 30% a year and on customers whose AI budgets it does not control.

The post ASML Has More Demand Than Machines. How It Allocates Them Is the Real Story appeared first on DataFLOQ.

items.title: Why Data Engineering Roles Stay Open So Long, and How Teams Fill the Gap in the Meantime
items.summary: The job ad went up in March. By October, nobody has signed. An analyst and a borrowed backend developer keep the reporting stack upright with late-night patches, while executives wonder aloud why last quarter’s revenue looks different in every dashboard. Plenty of companies know this scene. Data engineering vacancies routinely outlast openings for frontend, QA, or even DevOps roles, and the reasons are more structural than most hiring managers assume. So are the workarounds that extend your data team while you search. The Data Engineer Shortage Started Because Demand Grew Faster Than Anyone Could Train for the Job Picture a company’s information as water. Sales records, app clicks, payment logs, support tickets: each trickles in from a different source, and none of it is drinkable on arrival. Data engineers lay the pipes. They collect those streams, filter out the junk, and route everything to one reservoir where an analyst can build a report or an AI model can learn. If a joint leaks, everyone downstream drinks bad numbers. As professions go, this one is young. In 2017, Maxime Beauchemin (creator of the open-source scheduler Apache Airflow) published “The Rise of the Data Engineer,” an essay that helped give the discipline a name. Back then, plenty of firms still handed the work to whichever backend developer had spare hours. Universities lagged too; dedicated degrees remain scarce. So almost every senior practitioner today picked up the craft sideways, through trial, outages, and inherited systems. Appetite for that skill exploded anyway. Cloud migrations need it. So do analytics programs, and now every AI initiative that hopes to reach production. Postings for data engineers grew [VERIFY: year-over-year growth figure, e.g. from the Dice Tech Jobs Report or LinkedIn Jobs on the Rise], while the supply of experienced people crept along. Where the data engineer shortage really bites is seniority. A motivated junior can get comfortable with dbt or Snowflake inside a few months. Judgment is another matter. Knowing why a pipeline dies at 3 a.m., how a design will hold up under ten times today’s volume, which tempting shortcut becomes a six-figure rebuild: that comes only from years of scar tissue. People who carry it seldom browse job boards. What results is a seller’s talent market. Strong candidates juggle several offers and sign within days. Any company running a cautious, month-long process is bidding for a tiny pool against rivals who close in two weeks. Most Data Engineering Job Ads Describe Three Different People Skim ten postings for this role. A pattern surfaces fast: when a company isn’t sure what it needs, it asks for everything. A single ad can quietly merge the duties of a data engineer, an analytics engineer, and a machine learning engineer, then tack on “5+ years of experience” for good measure. A typical overloaded req bundles most of these: Pipeline orchestration: scheduling data jobs so they run in the right order (Apache Airflow, Dagster) Cloud data warehousing: designing large storage systems such as Snowflake, BigQuery, or Redshift Real-time streaming: processing data that arrives every second rather than in a nightly batch, often via Apache Kafka Data modeling: turning raw records into tables business users can actually query ML infrastructure: feeding clean data to AI models running in production Can one person cover all five? A handful can. Expect to pay for them like a small team. Worse is the silent attrition. Capable engineers scan a list like that, spot two gaps, and close the tab. Those who do apply then meet an applicant-tracking filter that rejects them over one missing keyword. Months pass. Eventually someone declares that “nobody qualified exists,” when the posting itself chased most of them away. Before writing the next ad, pin down the two or three skills this hire genuinely needs during their first six months. An Empty Data Engineering Seat Costs More Than the Salary You’re Saving On a budget spreadsheet, a vacancy looks almost free. No paycheck leaves the account. Finance is happy. Elsewhere, the bill keeps growing. Roadmaps slide: a dashboard launch waits, an AI pilot idles, a migration scoped for one quarter drags into three. Somebody steps in to keep data flowing, usually a backend developer or a senior analyst, and they’re good at quick patches. Patches from outside the specialty, though, accumulate into technical debt. Picture shortcuts that hold today and crack next spring, with repair costs far above what doing it right would have cost. Burnout follows. Covering two jobs works for a few weeks, maybe a quarter. After that, expect your most reliable stand-in to quietly update their LinkedIn. For data engineers, average time to hire sits around [VERIFY: average days to fill a data engineering role, e.g. from LinkedIn Talent Insights or a recruiting benchmark report]. Put a price on each of those weeks. Those numbers rarely appear next to the “saved” salary in budget reviews, but they’re usually bigger. Faster Data Engineering Hires Start With a Narrower Role and a Shorter Interview Process A stalled search rarely needs more money. The delay usually comes from scope, and from how slowly the company moves once someone good applies. Start with the scope. If you need one person to build pipelines and another to shape data for your analysts, you’re looking at two hires. A narrower brief pulls in more applicants and is easier to interview for. Next, be honest about what’s truly required on day one. Has the candidate run BigQuery or Redshift at scale but never touched Snowflake? That gap closes in a few weeks. Weak judgment about data quality or system design doesn’t close quickly at all, so that’s where screening should get strict. Speed is the part companies get wrong most often. A five-round process spread across six weeks loses finalists to employers who make an offer in two, and that’s how a perfectly reasonable hiring strategy ends up producing nobody. Three stages are enough for most teams: a technical screen, a practical exercise based on a problem you actually had, and a talk with future teammates. If a take-home task runs longer than two hours, pay for it (or drop it). It’s also worth looking past your own city. Remote hiring gives you access to deep engineering talent in Eastern Europe and Latin America. You might get three or four hours of overlap a day, and contracts across borders mean extra legal work. Many companies still find that easier to live with than an empty desk until next summer. Freelancers, Upskilling, and Staff Augmentation Each Solve a Different Part of the Gap Fixing the process won’t produce a permanent hire overnight. Reports still have to run, so most teams bring in temporary help. Each option covers one weakness and opens another. Freelancers are fastest when the task has clear edges. Through Toptal or Upwork, you can often have a contractor working on a broken ingestion job within days. What you give up is continuity. A freelancer may be serving three other clients, and when the contract ends, whatever they learned about your systems goes with them. They fit jobs with an obvious end, like moving one data source. Upskilling someone you already employ is slower, but you keep the result. A backend developer who knows your product can work through a structured course like DataTalksClub’s free Data Engineering Zoomcamp. Plan on several months before they’re independent. Their old work also needs a new owner, so for a while the gap partly just moves. The third route is a vendor that offers staff augmentation. Its engineers join your standups, commit to your repositories, and use your tools, while the vendor takes care of recruiting and payroll. If you need senior people in weeks, you can extend your data team this way while the permanent search continues. The downsides are real. You’ll usually pay more per hour than an equivalent employee would cost, and vendors differ a lot in quality. Knowledge can also end up living only in the heads of the external engineers. Required documentation and pairing with your own staff from week one help prevent that. In practice, plenty of companies mix all three. Contract engineers keep the important pipelines running, an internal developer learns next to them, and recruiters can keep looking without settling. Plan for a Long Data Engineering Search Before You Post the Job If a data engineering seat has been empty for six months, that doesn’t automatically mean your recruiters dropped the ball. In this market, searches often take that long. The companies that cope best simply assume it from the start. When the ad goes live, answer two questions. Who keeps the pipelines running until someone is hired? And how much will that cost? Then set a checkpoint, for example day 60. If the role is still open by that date, interim help starts without another round of meetings. Outside engineers can carry a data function for months, sometimes longer. Over years, though, a company that makes decisions based on data needs people on its own payroll who know where that data comes from and what usually breaks it.

items.title: Is Nvidia Too Powerful? Jensen Huang Responds
items.summary: Does the AI industry’s reliance on Nvidia pose a systemic risk? In an interview filmed on October 14 for an upcoming episode of The Circuit, CEO Jensen Huang responds. Huang has since acknowledged an affair, and US intelligence officials reportedly suspect the woman was recruited by Beijing to influence him. Nvidia’s board is now investigating. items.title: Why GCCs and Indian IT are Partnering at Enterprise Scale
items.summary: India’s global capability centres (GCCs) are taking on larger technology, product development and innovation mandates, raising questions about whether multinational companies will increasingly build capabilities in-house at the expense of Indian IT services firms. Workato believes the relationship is more likely to evolve into a partnership, with GCCs driving innovation and Indian IT companies bringing the scale, industry expertise and implementation capabilities needed to translate it into enterprise transformation. “I do not think one can really succeed without the other,” Shane Smith, Director and Global Head of Partner Success at Workato, tells AIM, describing the relationship between GCCs and Indian IT companies. While GCCs are gaining greater autonomy to develop technology and build specialised teams, implementing AI across large organisations requires integration with legacy systems, enterprise-wide governance and the ability to deploy solutions at scale. For Workato, an AI orchestration and governance platform, this creates an opportunity to bring GCCs, Indian IT services companies and technology providers into a common ecosystem. GCCs Bring Innovation; Indian IT Brings Scale Speaking to AIM, David Ng, Global VP, Partner, GTM and Alliances at Workato, mentions the company’s engagement with Indian IT firms is evolving beyond the traditional model in which service providers primarily supplied delivery capacity. Historically, Workato partnered with Indian IT companies to increase implementation capacity. Today, the company increasingly looks to these partners for innovation and industry-specific expertise. “Historically we partnered for delivery scale, but increasingly today we are partnering for the innovation our partners drive in this space,” Ng says. The distinction is important for GCCs. As multinational companies expand their India operations, these centres are increasingly expected to develop products, engineer AI solutions and solve business problems for global operations. However, the ability to develop a solution does not automatically translate into the ability to deploy and maintain it across a large enterprise. Ng says these partnerships allow companies to decide which capabilities to build internally and which to access through external providers. “ GCCs need scale, and scale comes with a component of risk. You have to decide what you want to build and what you want to buy. When you build, there is an element of risk and an element of maintenance. When you buy that capability, some of that is mitigated,” he states. Partnerships can also provide access to expertise beyond the immediate organisation, helping GCCs address problems they may not have identified internally. AI is Changing What Partners Bring to the Table The growing adoption of enterprise AI is creating a different set of requirements for technology partnerships. Enterprises need to connect AI models and applications with data spread across enterprise resource planning systems, customer relationship management platforms, databases, procurement systems and other business applications. Workato argues that this requires both technology infrastructure and specialised knowledge of how industries operate. Ng describes Workato as a horizontal platform that can be adapted to different industries, while its partners bring the vertical expertise needed to address specific business problems. “Where Workato is a strong horizontal platform, our partners layer strong vertical expertise and subject-matter expertise on top of our platform, helping us solve very unique industry problems,” he states. Partners such as Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Tech Mahindra, Infosys and HCLTech contribute implementation resources as well as knowledge of industry-specific requirements. In banking, this could involve know-your-customer processes or fraud detection. In retail, it could involve inventory management. In insurance, partners can help identify operational gaps where AI could deliver measurable value. Ng says these companies bring three broad capabilities, like delivery skills, industry-related subject-matter expertise, and distribution and credibility. Their role is particularly relevant as enterprises attempt to move AI from isolated applications into core business processes. Without reliable connections to enterprise data and systems, AI investments risk remaining limited to experimentation, knowledge retrieval or peripheral productivity tools. Workato’s proposition is that connectivity, execution and governance must work together before enterprises can safely allow AI agents to interact with business-critical systems. Why GCCs May Still Need Indian IT Companies The growing autonomy of GCCs raises a central question: if multinational companies can recruit specialised talent and build their own AI capabilities in India, why do they need Indian IT services firms? For Workato, the answer lies in the difference between developing a capability and scaling its deployment. A GCC may build a solution for a particular business function, but implementing it across multiple systems, business units and geographies can require substantial engineering resources and industry expertise. External partners can help provide that capacity without requiring the enterprise to build every capability internally. Ng says Workato itself follows a similar model . As a product and platform company, it wants to concentrate its investments on improving its technology rather than managing every customer implementation. “We do not want to own the end-to-end implementation of our platform for every customer, because we want to continue investing in product innovation. That is where our investment should go, not into hiring more people to deliver the platform for a customer,” he says. The arrangement also creates a commercial incentive for Indian IT services firms. Partners can earn services revenue from large transformation projects while gaining access to technology that supports their customer engagements. Workato, in turn, gains access to implementation capacity and industry knowledge. Ng describes the arrangement as a “give-and-take relationship”, adding that partners play a significant role in helping Workato operate efficiently as a product organisation. This suggests that the growth of GCCs does not necessarily eliminate the need for external technology providers. Instead, it could change the nature of the relationship, with in-house teams focusing on product ownership and innovation while partners contribute implementation scale, specialised capabilities and transformation expertise. India is Becoming the Centre of Enterprise AI Innovation Workato’s decision to deepen its presence in India is tied to where enterprises are building their AI capabilities. Ng says conversations with customers globally increasingly point towards India when discussing where solutions are being developed. “Every time they talk about the problem they are trying to solve and where that solution is being built, it points back to India. That is why we want to be as close as possible to where innovation is being built, and why we are hiring in India and walking the hallways where this innovation is happening,” he states. The company is looking for a combination of domain expertise and AI solutioning capabilities, particularly among AI architects who must integrate workflows into industry-specific processes and legacy systems. “An intersection of functional and technical skills works best in such scenarios,” Ng says. For GCCs, this intersection is increasingly important as they take on responsibilities that extend beyond conventional technology support. Building AI solutions requires an understanding of both the technology and the business process being redesigned. Indian IT companies can complement these capabilities by bringing experience across industries, implementation resources and relationships with enterprise decision-makers. Indian IT Firms Must Adapt to the Next Phase of Transformation Smith states that the Indian IT services companies have repeatedly adapted to changes in technology and customer expectations, and he does not view the rise of GCCs as an event that will make their skills redundant. “These organisations have always adapted to the current and have always been trusted by their customers to help them navigate the future. That is how I look at it,” he says. He adds that Indian IT firms would continue to help customers navigate the next phase of enterprise technology transformation. The opportunity, however, depends on how effectively these firms adapt to the changing requirements of enterprise AI. Traditional delivery capacity alone may not be sufficient when customers want industry-specific AI solutions, integration with business-critical systems and measurable returns from their investments . The company’s view is that GCCs and Indian IT services firms are not necessarily competing for the same role. As GCCs take on more innovation-led work, Indian IT companies can move towards becoming strategic transformation partners, bringing the expertise and scale required to implement that innovation across enterprises.
